conditions.text: In the fiscal field a number of measures are being taken to strengthen government finances. Every effort is being made to hold down ordinary expenditures and a program has been initiated to improve collections from existing taxes. Moreover, the budget for the current fiscal year - 4 - ANNEX (1969/70), which was approved in August 1969, included a number of new revenue measures which are estimated to increase government revenue by about Af 350 million in 1969/70 and by about Af 480 million on an annual basis. These measures include increases in the prices of gasoline and diesel oil, a revision of the income tax law, adjustments in road tolls, the introduction of a motor vehicle registration fee and a monopoly duty on imported tea, and increased sale of government land and other property. In addition to these measures, the Government has recently taken administrative measures to increase the effective level of import duties to yield about Af 120 million on an annual basis.

conditions.text: In view of the relatively slow growth in bank credit over the last four years, the continued underutilization of resources and the recent decline of prices, it is believed that a somewhat more liberal credit policy than that pursued in 1347 (1965/69) is feasible without the re-emergence of inflationary pressures. While the credit needs of the private sector to accommodate an expansion in production and exports are expected to be at an annual rate of Af 250 million (about the level of 1347), the public sector requirement will be somewhat larger particularly in the first half of 1348 (1969/70). conditions.text: Prior to and during a recent visit by a Fund staff team to Afghanistan, the Government reviewed economic developments and prospects in light of the objectives of the stabilization programs initiated in May 1965 and June 1966, and of the aims of Afghanistan's current development program. Over the past three years the main emphasis in government policy has been on strengthening public sector finances and on reducing public sector reliance on the banking system. In addition, the exchange system was simplified and some incentives were provided for major exports. The implementation of stabilization measures produced substantial results in the form of reduced pressures on resources. In the three years ended March 21, 1968, public sector deficits were moderate whereas in -the preceding three years bank financing of the public sector was equivalent to about one quarter of government expenditures. However, progress in other directions has not been as satisfactory as hoped. In particular, Afghanistan's major exports have not increased and the external financial position has continued to be strained. Although the free market rate for the afghani has been relatively stable for the last three years, foreign exchange reserves have continued to decline.

conditions.clause: the tax and subsidy measures described in paragraph 4 of the attached memorandum are not adopted and maintained, or
conditions.text: The Afghan authorities recognize that in the exchange field the most effective measure to strengthen the balance of payments would be to change the rate of exchange applicable to the proceeds of cotton, cotton seeds, karakul and wool exports from the official rate to the free market rate. It would initially be necessary to impose exchange taxes on the proceeds of these exports in order to reduce the budgetary burden involved in the exchange rate adjustment and in order to preclude windfall profits. However, legislative approval of tax measures may prove to be -4- ANNEX a time consuming process. The measures described in the attached memorandum have been decided upon in order to avoid this possible delay. It is the intent of the Government to seek legislative approval at an early date for the tax measures necessary for the implementation of the change in the exchange system described in this paragraph.

The Argentine economy is passing through a difficult period. In the 12 months ended in April 1976 the cost of living rose by almost 800 per cent and wholesale prices by over 900 per cent, the balance of payments deficit was over US$700 million, the budget deficit was equivalent to about 78 per cent of expenditure or 13 per cent of GDP, and economic activity declined by 5-10 per cent. The new Government which took office on March 24, 1976 adopted a program to reverse these trends as quickly as possible. The program, announced on April 2, was immediately successful in containing inflation and in eliminating the threat of a default on external payments. Wholesale prices, which had increased by 54 per cent in March, rose by 27 per cent in April and by less than 5 per cent in May; and the increase in the cost of living declined from 38 per cent in March to 35 per cent in April, 13 per cent in May and less than 3 per cent in June. conditions.text: The program to achieve economic stability rwill include a reform of the exchange system. The Government has decided to adopt the following changes. (a) The existing dual exchange markets, official and free, will be eliminated and replaced by a single exchemge market fcr the peso which wia be free of all direct restrictions. Apart from the. intervention in the exchange market described in (b) below, the exchange rate will be determined by the free play of market forces. This means that the Government will not ensure that exchange transactions will be based on the par value under the new exchange system. It is the intention of the Argentine Government to proceed to a fixed unitary rate and to declare a new par value as soon as the internal financial situation has been consolidated and external equilibrium attained. (b) Drawings against the balance of payments loans, including drawlngs under the stand-by arrangement with the Fund, and Central Bank intervention in the free market with these funds will be limited to US$155 million during the period of the. stand-by arrangement. conditions.text: With the objective of reducing the rate of inflation to 8 per cent in 1979/80, we intend to allow for an expansion of total liquidity of 15 per cent during the stand-by period, a rate we consider to be consistent with our growth target of 7 per cent. In line with our forecast balance of payments deficit in 1979/80, we intend to limit total credit expansion to 20 per cent. Taking into account seasonal credit needs, total credit (i.e., claims of the banking system on the Government less government deposits plus claims of the banking system on the rest of the public sector and on the private sector) which amounted to Tk 27,323 million on April 27, 1979, will be limited to no more than Tk 30,100 million during the period up to September 30, 1979, Tk 32,800 million during the period up to January 31, 1980, and Tk 33,150 million during the period up to May 31, 1980. Within this overall ceiling, the sum of net credit to the Government and gross credit to the rest of the public sector, which amounted to Tk 17,330 million on April 27, 1979, will be limited to no more than Tk 19,700 million during the period up to September 30, 1979 and Tk 21,000 million during the period up to January 31, 1980; thereafter, such credit will decline to no more than Tk 20,750 million on May 31, 1980. We intend to take prompt corrective measures if developments suggest that the above ceilings and subceilings may be exceeded.

conditions.text: Bangladesh has relied extensively on external assistance to finance imports, and will have to continue to do so in the foreseeable future. Unpredictable changes in the domestic supply of foodgrains in the past have also required their imports on commercial credit terms. Unexpected shortfall in foodgrain production this year and lower import of foodgrains under aid program have made it necessary to consider additional import on an emergency basis. It is foreseen that imports will be made on both cash and commercial credit terms. By the end of 1978/79, outstanding external debt is estimated to amount to about $2.9 billion, and service payments with respect to this debt during 1978/79 to $96 million. The estimated total debt service payments in 1978/79 would be equivalent to about 17 per cent of the estimated merchandise exports. As the low ratio of service payments to outstanding debt indicates, it: has been our policy to obtain foreign assistance on concessional terms and in long maturities. However, we recognize that the level of service payments is already relatively high in relation to our export earnings. Given the need to continue to rely on external assistance in the coming years and our desire to maintain the share of export earnings available to finance rising import requirements, we plan to continue to adopt a cautious external debt management policy. conditions.text: The cornerstone of the Government's financial program is its fiscal policy. Bolivia's economy is to a large extent an export-oriented economy but, in recent years, export producers have been prevented from contributing their share to government revenues by their weak competitive position. Under the new conditions, export producers, both public and private, will now be able to contribute to government revenues through the medium of the 20 per cent tax which has been established on exports of minerals, metals, petroleum and petroleum derivatives, cotton, cattle and meat, and the 15 per cent tax which has been established on all other exports. At the same time, certain other new taxes have been established, a major program of improvement in tax administration is being undertaken, and studies have been initiated with a view to carrying out a thoroughgoing reform of Bolivia's tax system. Finally, the Government's methods of budgeting, cash management, and expenditure control and policy are to be improved through the introduction of legislation which has been prepared in these fields. These measures will, for the first time in several years, produce a sizable current account surplus which, together with the proceeds of foreign development loans, will permit an expanded level of public investment. During 1971 and the first ten months of 1972, the Central Government's substantial credit needs, coupled with those of the private sector, led to an expansion in bank credit far in excess of the economy's ability to absorb this rise in credit. In 1973, with the finances of the Government producing a surplus, the monetary authorities will be in a position to provide a growing level of resources for private investment, while minimizing price inflation and providing for a moderate recuperation in the level of net international reserves. To this end, limits have been established on the net domestic assets of the Central Bank, reduced by its deposit obligations to the rest of the banking system. These limits are laid down in Table 2.

conditions.clause: the limits on the incurrence of new foreign indebtedness of the public sector referred to in paragraph 8 and further described in Table 3 of the annexed letter are exceeded; or
conditions.text: Over the past three years, service payments on Bolivia's external public debt have risen markedly. This increase has reflected not only the expiration of grace periods on a large number of development loans, but also a deterioration in the maturity structure of the debt arising from the increased use of medium-term suppliers' credits to finance public investment projects., The Government is determined to maintain strict control over the foreign indebtedness of the public sector and to limit short- and medium-term borrowing with a view to improving the maturity structure of Bolivia's external public debt. To this end, all foreign credits to the public sector will continue to be subject to prior authorization by the National Economic and Planning Council. Limits will be observed for the authorization of such new debt of at least 1 year and less than 15 years' maturity. These limits are set down in Table 3.

conditions.clause: the intention stated in the last sentence of paragraph 9 of the annexed letter is not carried out
conditions.text: Bolivia's exchange system contains no restrictions, foreign exchange being made available freely to any buyer for current and capital purposes. During 1971, some exchange restrictions were introduced de facto, but these restrictions failed to stem the demand for foreign exchange and, rather, undermined public confidence in the stability of the peso. These restrictive practices have now been abandoned and, in fact, the authorities have abolished the reporting form on which purchasers of foreign exchange were required to state the purpose for which exchange was being sought. The Government is firm in its determination to maintain an exchange system free of practices which would be inconsistent with Bolivia's obligations under the Fund's Articles of Agreement except as provided in the Fund's decisions concerning wider margins.

Every effort will be made to improve the finances of the major state enterprises and to keep the latter's access to central bank credit within moderate amounts. However, neither COMIBOL nor YPFB will during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement increase its outstanding indebtedness to the Monetary Department of the Central Bank, except for any interest accrual debited to COMIBOL as of the end of 1963 and as of June 30, 1964. -'5

conditions.text: The legal reserve requirements for the deposit obligations of the private commercial banks will during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement be maintained at a minimum of 35 per cent against all sight deposit obligations and at a minimum of 25 per cent against all time and savings deposit obligations. These minimum legal reserve requirements will apply to obligations denominated either in Bolivian pesos or in foreign currencies. As heretofore, only reserve deposits with the Monetary Department of the Central Bank and currency in vaults up to onefifth of the total will qualify as legal reserves of the commercial banks against their peso liabilities and only reserve deposits in foreign exchange with the Monetary Department of the Central Bank will qualify as legal reserve against the commercial bank liabilities denominated in foreign currencies. The existing penalties for legal reserve deficiencies will be maintained and strictly enforced. The Banking Department of the Central Bank will continue to be exempt from the legal reserve requirements.

conditions.text: The Monetary Department of the Central Bank will limit the expansion of its credit and investment operations to an amount compatible with internal price stability and balance of payments equilibrium. Accordingly, the net amount of its total loans and investments less the sum of its obligations on account of (i) counterpart funds from foreign grants and loans; (ii) deposits of the government; and (iii) reserve deposits of the commercial banks, will not exceed the level of July 31, 1963 by more than $b25 million until November 30, 1963 and by more than $b40 million from December 1, 1963 until the expiration of the stand-by arrangement. It is understood, however, that all contributions to international institutions will not be subject to these limits. The above limits will be modified only in agreement with the International Monetary Fund.

conditions.text: The monetary budget approved by the National Monetary Council for 1972 is designed to permit an expansion of bank credit consistent with a projected rise in prices of 15 per cent and growth in real output of 8-9 per cent. In order to limit the growth in the money supply to around 24 per cent, while allowing for a moderate further rise in international reserves, the authorities have established a program to maintain firm control over the net domestic credit of the monetary authorities. According to this program, the net domestic assets of the monetary authorities (defined as the sum of the currency issue, the Bank of Brazil's private sight and time deposit liabilities, and the commercial bankst voluntary deposits with the Bank of Brazil minus net foreign reserves), which were Cr$8,8 04 million on September 30, 1971, will not exceed Cr$8,136 million during the first quarter of 1972; Cr$10,100 million during the second quarter of 1972; Cr$10,408 million during the third quarter of 1972; and Cr$13,605 million during the fourth quarter of 1972. Fiscal cash expenditures are planned at NCr$13, 6 53 million, or slightly less than 19 per cent above the level registered in 1968; in real terms, cash expenditures this year are programed to be about the same as in the previous year. In addition to the limit of NCr$528 million on the fiscal cash deficit for 1969 as a whole, the following quarterly limits have been established: the cumulative cash deficit this year is not to exceed NCr$874 million by March 31, 1969; NCr$993 million by June 30, 1969; and NCr$907 million by September 30, 1969. If the trends should indicate that the deficit will rise above the limits that have been established, either because of a shortfall in revenues or an increase in expenditures above the level now planned, the authorities will take action to correct the situation.

conditions.text: The monetary budget approved by the authorities for 1968 envisages a major reduction in the rate of increase of bank credit from the one registered last year, and it is designed to be consistent with further progress toward stabilization and a recovery in foreign reserves. In accordance with these objectives, the net domestic credit of the monetary authorities will not exceed NCr$8,865 million during the second quarter of 1968; NCr$9,060 million during the third quarter of 1968; and NCr$9,600 million during the fourth quarter of 1968.

conditions.text: It is the intention of the authorities to pursue in 1968 an exchange rate policy--in conjunction with credit and wage policies--that will enable them to improve their foreign reserve position and to maintain adequate incentives for exports, particularly for nontraditional export products. The monetary budget envisages an increase in net foreign assets of $125 million over the full year. Measured from the base date of December 31, 1967, net foreign assets are to improve by at least $65 million by June 30, 1968; $95 million by September 30, 1968; and $125 million by December 31, 1968. The monetary authorities' forward exchange liabilities, which are included in the calculation of the net foreign asset position, rose very rapidly in the second half of 1967 when the cruzeiro came under severe pressure. However, such liabilities are expected to decline sharply in 1968, on the strength of the improvement projected in the balance of payments situation and because the authorities have initiated a policy of exercising caution in entering into forward sales of exchange. To the extent that forward exchange liabilities decline to a level below the amount outstanding at the end of 1967, the net foreign asset goals described above will be increased accordingly.

conditions.text: In 1968, Brazil eliminated the last of its swap arrangements, which only five years ago totaled nearly $4CO million, and it is the policy of the authorities not to enter into any new swap contracts. To continue the improvement of its medium-term foreign debt position, the authorities intend to pursue during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement a policy of limiting authorizations for the public sector of new suppliers' credits with a maturity of less than eight years to the amount of the amortization of existing suppliers' credits. Recently, the Central Bank authorized the commercial banks and certain other financial institutions to contract short-term credits from abroad for relending in Brazil, with the amolnuri permitted for each institution being related to -8its capital and with the explicit provision that the exchange rate risk must be borne by the domestic borrower. The authorities are following closely the trends in operations under this new facility, and they will take action to curb its use if it should appear that such indebtedness abroad is rising too rapidly.

conditions.text: The monetary budget for 1968 envisages a large contractionary impact from coffee operations, offsetting part of the expansion in bank credit from the monetary authorities for other purposes. This projection of the movement of the coffee account is based on (1) the expectation that purchases of surplus coffee by the Brazilian Coffee Institute will be rather small in view of the comparatively small size of the 1967/68 coffee crop and the even smaller crop forecast for the 1968/69 coffee year, and (2) the intention of the authorities to limit to only moderate amounts the increases in the cruzeiro return paid to exporters and the domestic support price that will be madq effective in mid-1968. Moreover, the authorities recently raised the price at which the Brazilian Coffee Institute sells coffee for domestic consumption, and further adjustments are envisaged during the course of this year.

conditions.text: In recent months, high marginal reserve requirements have been applied against the deposit liabilities of private commercial banks in order to moderate the growth in credit, particularly to prevent an undue expansion in bank credit based on the large increase in private sector liquidity that occurred late in 1967 and the inflow of capital that has been taking place as a consequence of the adjustment of the exchange rate early in 1968. Late in March, it was decided to terminate these marginal reserve requirements, effective from April 5, 1968, but at the same time most of the basic reserve requirements were increased. It has been calculated that these changes will result in a higher average required ratio than the one yielded by the previous basic requirements. For 1968 as a whole, the program has been based on the basic requirements that were in force prior to the recent changes. The authorities plan to proceed cautiously in reducing the ratio of the compulsory cash reserves of the commercial banks to their deposit liabilities toward the level prevailing i December 1967, with the pace of such reduction depending on credit conditions and price and production developments. conditions.text: With regard to other aspects of exchange policy, it is the intention of the authorities to avoid imposing new restrictions on the making of payments and transfers for current international transactions or the introduction of new multiple currency practices. In this connection, the provision of exchange cover from the monetary authorities for the private commercial banks will be reintroduced at an early date. It is the policy of the authorities to continue moving toward a multilateral payments system on a nondiscriminatory basis, and to this end they have in recent years terminated, or made arrangements for the termination of, a number of bilateral payments agreements, including some with members of the Fund. Apart from their own efforts to terminate some of the existing bilateral payments agreements, the authorities are willing to participate in multinational discussions sponsored by the Fund for that purpose. In 1967, the authorities implemented major import liberalization measures, consisting of the transfer of import commodities from the restrictive Special Category to the General Category and the adoption of a new tariff law that provided for a general reduction in duties. It is the policy of the authorities to maintain the over-all liberalization achieved.

conditions.text: Over the last two years, Brazil has succeeded in achieving a significant improvement in its foreign exchange reserve position and in simplifying considerably its exchange system. An important factor in this result has been the marked improvement in Brazil's export performance. Nontraditional exports increased sharply in 1965 and they continued to grow in 1966, although at a lower rate. The authorities have maintained a unified exchange rate structure and the Brazilian Government intends to pursue the same policy in the coming year. Tomaintain a sound balance of payments position, reliance will be placed on an integrated set of credit, fiscal, and exchange rate policies. While the rate of increase of costs has been slowed down considerably over the past two years--particularly through a marked improvement in the control over wages--increases are still taking place. The authorities expect that further progress will be made in the coming year in slowing down the rate of cost increases, and measures are being taken to reduce certain cost elements, but until costs are stabilized it will be necessary to continue to pursue a flexible exchange rate policy in order to avoid the emergence of balance of payments difficulties or stagnation in economic activity. To assist them in setting the exchange rate, the authorities have established balance of payments performance targets. conditions.text: In 1966, the Brazilian authorities moved further toward liberalizing outgoing foreign exchange payments. It is the policy of the Brazilian Government to maintain the progress achieved over the past two years toward establishing a payments system virtually free of restrictions. To this end, it will remain its intention not to impose new restrictions in the making of payments and transfers for current international transactions. The Brazilian authorities have also taken further steps to simplify the exchange rate system through the elimination of a number of taxes on foreign exchange transactions that had constituted multiple currency practices. However, because of weaknesses in the customs administrative machinery, the tax recently imposed on an export commodity 9 referred to in paragraph 7 above has been levied in a manner that might be interpreted as giving rise to a multiple currency practice. Should this turn out to be the case, the Brazilian authorities will replace it by one outside the exchange system as soon as feasible. The Brazilian Government intends to review the possibility of replacing the export taxes levied through the exchange system by taxes collected through the fiscal system. To consolidate the unification of the exchange rate structure, it will be the Government's policy not to introduce new multiple currency practices.

conditions.text: The policy of the Brazilian Government continued to be to move toward a multilateral payments system on a nondiscriminatory basis. To this end, it has recently terminated a bilateral payments agreement with a country that is a member of the Fund, and the elimination of a number of other such agreements is under active consideration. The authorities have, moreover, removed the only remaining discriminatory exchange practices which had consisted of the differential in the guarantee deposit requirement applicable to exchange transactions covered by bilateral payments agreements.

At the same time the authorities will continue taking steps to encourage the public to place funds not currently needed in savings deposits of the Bank of Brazil, commercial banks, and financial institutions, so as to permit sound financing of domestic investment. conditions.text: The Brazilian Government has succeeded in unifying the exchange market and intends to place major reliance on the exchange rate to achieve a sound improvement in its balance of payments and foreign exchange reserve position. Accordingly, the exchange rates quoted by the Bank of Brazil will follow the fundamental market trends. Interventions by the Band of Brazil rill be designed to smooth out fluctuations arising from temporary and seasonal factors. Moreover, steps will be taken to broaden the exchange market operated by the commercial banks by shifting, to the maximum extent feasible, purchases of foreign exchange for imports and other payments frora the Bank of Brazil to the commercial banks. (a) In order to avoid that the Banlk of Brazil's rate is affected by speculative movements, the adjustment of its rate for foreign exchange sales to the commercial banks' rate may be delayed by as much as one week and the rate may be set, in terms of cruzeiros per U.S. dollar, as much as 2*5 per cent below the commaercial banks' rate. (b) In carrying out its policy with regard to foreign exchange commit~ments, the Bank of Brazil will ensure that the net foreign exchange assets of the monetary authorities, defined in a separate mlemorandum, at the end of each ,month in 1965 will be, in U.S. dollar terms, equal to, or higher than, that existing at the end of October 1964.

consultation

The Government of Burundi believes that the policies set forth in this letter are adequate to achieve the objectives of the program but will take any further measures that may become appropriate for this purpose. During the period of the stand-by arrangement, the Government of Burundi will consult the Fund on the adoption of any measures that may become appropriate at its own initiative or whenever the Managing Director requests such consultations because the criteria set forth in paragraph 15 are not observed or because he considers that consultations on the program are desirable. In addition, after the expiration of the period of the stand-by arrangement and while any Fund holdings of Burundi's currency above the first credit tranche include currency resulting from purchases under this stand-by arrangement, the Government of Burundi will consult the Fund periodically at its own initiative or at the-request of the Managing Director concerning Burundi's balance of payments policies. Very truly yours, /S/ Joseph Hicuburundi Minister of Finance Bank of the Republic of Burundi /s/ Bonaventure Kidwingira President /S/ is/ Patrice Nsababaganwa Raymond Setukuru Diector Director

conditions.text: In order to meet the seasonal requirements of the Treasury for the financing of the ordinary budget, the Government of Burundi may increase its indebtedness vis-a-vis the banking system but the net claims of the banking system on the Government which amounted to FBu 811.6 million on December 31, 1969 shall not exceed FBu 1,100 million until June 30, 1970. This net indebtedness shall be reduced to FBu 780 million by September 30, 1970 and shall not exceed FBu 812 million until December 31, 1970 and FBu 948 million until March 31, 1971.

conditions.text: Burundi's allocation of Special Drawing Rights is held and managed by the Bank of the Republic of Burundi. It is recorded on the assets side in an account denominated "holdings of Special Drawing Rights", and is part of foreign assets in the same category as gold, foreign currencies and other external claims. The domestic contraliability of SDR allocation will remain on the liabilities side in a blocked account with the Bank of the Republic of Burundi. In view of the improvement in the reserve position mainly as a result of the allocation of SDR's, the Bank of the Republic will extend a special advance which is not to exceed FBu 70 million. This advance will be credited to a special deposits account of the Government and will be used only to cover the local currency contribution to development projects financed by foreign aid.

conditions.text: The monetary authorities will continue to follow a cautious policy with respect to credit to the private sector. The credits excluded from the ceiling are mainly for exports and will be closely scrutinized by the Bank of the Republic of Burundi.

conditions.text: In the field of external settlements, the adoption of a new and uniform exchange rate and far-reaching liberaliz~~ion measures have brought foreign trade to a more satisfactory level and resulted in a restocking of the traditional commercial channels. These measures have restored confidence in business circles and, through keener competition, have contributed to price stability. As anticipated, the 1966 balance of payments deficit exceeded that of the previous year and reached $3.5 million. The initial impact of the liberalization measures on the balance of payments began to subside toward the middle of 1966, and available information seems ttb indicate that import payments in 1967 will fall slightly short of those of 1966. Moreover, the drain on the liquidity of the private sector, which is expected in 1967, makes it seem probable that transfers on account of profit and dividend remittances in 1967 vlill be less than in the previous year. To this end, total credit to the private sector will not exceed FBu 435 million at the end of March and April; FBu 875 million at the end of May; FBu 1,200 million at the end of June, July, August, and September; FBu 625 million at the end of October and November; FBu 435 million at the end of December 1967; and FBu 435 million at the end of January and February 1968. To meet credit requirements occasioned by the anticipated increase in coffee exports, the seasonal maximum figures of the above ceilings have been increased by FBu 100 million over those provided for in the 1966 stand-by arrangement. These ceilings are based on the assumption that the coffee crop will be 15,000 tons. If coffee exports should exceed this amount, the ceilings on credit to the private sector will be raised after cabled consultation and agreement with the Fund.

conditions.text: In the past year, Chile implemented a major liberalization of the exchange and trade system. The most important modifications involved the elimination of the 10,000 per cent import deposit requirement for most goods in the permitted import list; a substantial shortening of the compulsory waiting period for import payments; a liberalization of the quantitative restrictions on travel and family remittances; and a reduction in import duties from a level of 200-220 per cent to a maximum of 140 per cent. While Chile will not be able to continue this pace of liberalization due to the serious constraint imposed by the decline in copper prices, it is the authorities' firm resolve not to fall back on the introduction of new restrictions or on the intensification of the existing ones to cope with the balance of payments problem. Accordingly, in 1975, there will be no introduction of additional multiple currency practices or new restrictions nor intensification of existing restrictions on trade or payments for current international transactions. Moreover, all exchange for import payments will be made available no later than 120 days from the date of settlement in escudos. The authorities plan no removal of items from the permitted import list and no new import items will be made subject to the 10,000 per cent import deposit. During 1975, the authorities will continue to process promptly all applications for permitted imports and no bona fide import application will be rejected.

conditions.text: In the exchange field, the Government's intention is to unify the two existing markets as soon as circumstances permit. In both markets a flexible exchange rate policy will be pursued and no additional multiple currency practices will be established. All trade and trade-connected transactions, all operations of the Government and other public entities, and certain other invisible and capital transactions will continue to pass through the banking market. All exchange transactions in the banking market will continue to be conducted at unitary buying and selling rates. All residual exchange transactions will continue to pass through the brokers' market, and the existing controls on payments through this market will be limited to checking capital movements with a minimum of restrictions on current invisible transactions. Exchange policies will continue to be applied in a nondiscriminatory manner.

conditions.text: In recent years Chile has made considerable progress toward eliminating arrears on import payments and removing exchange and trade restrictions. Now the immediate concern of the Government on the external side is to strengthen the balance of payments situation, which at present precludes further significant liberalization. However, there will be no intensification of restrictions on current transactions for balance of payments -5reasons. Specifically, the compulsory deferment period for import payments will not be increased beyond 60 days from the date of shipment, and the Central Bank will not extend the existing period for forward delivery of its'sales of exchange. Moreover, to avoid any excessive delay in import payments, the existing list of imports for which importers are required to contract exchange cover within 50 days of shipment will be maintained, the intention being to increase the list and shorten the period as circumstances permit. ' As regards trade, there will be no intensification of existing import restrictions by removal of items from the permitted import list, and import applications will continue to be processed promptly. No item on the present permitted import list will be made subject to a rate of advance import deposit higher than that which it at present incurs with the exception of a few items whicdh for other than balance of payments reasons may possibly be made subject to the highest deposit rate.

conditions.text: With the help of the policies described in this letter, the Chilean authorities intend to bring about equilibrium in the balance of payments over 1968. Accordingly, there will be no reduction in the net foreign reserve position of the banking system over 1968 as a whole. To ensure the achievement of this objective and in the light of seasonal factors in the balance of payments, quarterly targets for changes in the net foreign exchange reserves of the banking system have been established: any reduction over the first three months of 1968 will not exceed $10 million; there will be no reduction over the first six months of 1968; and any reduction over the first nine months will not exceed $10 million. The above foreign reserve targets will be fully adjusted by the amount of any variation of actual over projected exchange receipts from the large copper companies to cover their domestic costs and taxes. These receipts are projected to amount to a cumulativ e $80 million in the first three months of 1968; a cumulative $165 million in the first six months of 1968; a cumulative $245 million in the first nine months of 1968; and a cumulative $340 million in 1968 as a whole.

conditions.text: The following are relevant aspects of the policies which the Goverrnment of Chile intends to pursue. In the exchange field, tiwo separate exchange markets will be maintained until such time as circumstances permit their reunification. In both markets, a flexible exchange rate policy will be pursued and no additional multiple currency practices will be established. All trade and trade-connected exchange transactions as well as all operations of the Government and other public entities will continue to pass through the banking market. The Central Bank will intervene in this market only to smooth out the effects of temporary pressures and will make every effort to eliminate any undue spread between the spot and futures rates in the lanking market. The brokers' market will continue to be confined to private capital transactions and residual current invisible transactions, and the existing controls in this market vill be limited to checking capital movements with a minimum of restriction on current invisible transactions. conditions.text: The Chilean authorities intend, by the pursuit of prudent monetary policies, to avoid future pressures on the balance of payments and on the domestic price level. Accordingly, with the exclusions listed below, the difference between the domestic assets of the Central Bank (including interest earned but not paid) and the sum of its capital and surplus accounts and its obligations on account of official deposits, P.L. 480 counterpart fund deposits and promissory notes to banks will at no time during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement be permitted to exceed the level on February 13, 1964 by more than EO 135 million. The following Central Bank operations will be excluded from the ceiling: (i) new subscription payments to the capital of international lending institutions; (ii) new loans and investments of the Central Bank made with the escudo counterpart funds from special foreign loans and credits received for relending to the private or public sector directly or through other financial intermediaries; and (iii) new revaluations of the Central Bank's foreign currency accounts. However, any release of reserve deposits of banks that may be authorized during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement, in accordance with paragraph 12 below, will be counted against this ceiling.

conditions.text: Established commercial banks and the Banco del Estado are currently subject to the following legal reserve requirements: (i) a basic requirement of 20 per cent against their demand deposit obligations in escudos and foreign currencies; (ii) a basic requirement of 8 per cent against their time deposit obligations in escudos and foreign currencies; and (iii) a requirement of 57 per cent against all increases in their deposit obligations in escudos over their average level during the period April 13-25, 1959. Banks that have only recently commenced operations in Chile are subject to a preferential legal reserve requirement against their demand and time deposit obligations in escudos, equal to the average rate applicable to the established banks during the -7preceding month, until such time as their combined deposit obligations in escudos reach the level of their capital and surplus. The legal reserve requirements are mainly satisfied by reserve deposits with the Central Bank and currency in the vaults of the banks, but some substitution of selected credit and investment operations by the banks for cash reserves has been authorized. It is the intention of the Chilean authorities not to reduce these legal reserve requirements below their current levels, and not to authorize any new substitution of selected credit and investment operations by the banks for cash reserves. conditions.text: So as to improve the effectiveness of credit control and to limit the total volume of credit to a level compatible with economic -3stability, the following measures are being taken: (a) The Government will eliminate the peso advance deposits for imports in the near future. An adequate level of advance deposit requirements in dollars and dollar Treasury bills, however, will be maintained to freeze, in effect, the current level of balances in dollar deposits and dollar Treasury bills used to meet advance import deposits. This step is necessary to prevent the.release of the existing dollar deposits with the Central Bar'k and to eliminate the need of the Government of internal financing in 1959. conditions.text: On the receipts side, revenues from existing taxes are currently estimated to amount to Chil$441 billion in 1959. The Government has introduced additional revenue measures in Congress, including new sales taxes and modifications of the income tax, in the same bill as that increasing wages and salaries of public employees. These measures are expected to yield Chil$62 billion on an annual basis and Chil$45 billion in 1959. In addition, the Government plans to eliminate the present prohibition on imports so as to permit all goods to be freely imported. At the same time, the Government will introduce import surcharges, collected at customs, which are estimated to yield about Chilt25 billion in 1959. Chile will discuss these surcharges with the GATT. The Government intends to eliminate these su,-harges as soon as an improved tariff structure is introduced in 1960. In the meantime, the surcharges will be kept under continuous review, Lastly, the Government expects to receive foreign credits in an amount sufficient to balance the Government's budgetary cash deficit in 1959. With government expenditures fully covered by current revenue and foreign credits, Central Bank credit to the Government will not exceed at any time during 1959 the level outstanding as of the end of 1958. conditions.text: The structural disequilibrium of the Colombian balance of payments, the still weak international reserve position, the importance of minimizing capital flight and speculative operations, and the uncertainties in the -6 world coffee market, make it necessary for Colombia to maintain the machinery of exchange control. It will continue to be administered in accordance with our international obligations, in particular the Articles of Agreement of the International Monetary Fund which were approved by the Colombian Congress in Law 96 of 1945. Progress will be made toward the simplification of the exchange system by timely application of the relevant provisions of Decree-Law 444 of 1967. During the period of the stand-by arrangement there will be no delays in foreign exchange payments for imports or freight beyond the 20-day period implied in the advance deposit requirement for exchange payments. Moreover, the authorities will speed up the administrative processes for the registration of foreign capital and will make every effort to bring up to date and maintain on a current basis payments for current transactions which are now transacted in the capital market, such as interest, royalty and profit remittances.

conditions.text: Expanding production and rising employment levels require reimbursable import registrations at the minimum levels set forth in annexed Table 1. Although it would have been desirable to aim at larger import volumes for the sake of attaining a more rapid economic growth, it does not seem possible to do so given the reduced foreign exchange earnings from coffee exports, the urgent need to strengthen the international reserve position and the sizable foreign commercial indebtedness incurred in 1966 while imports were exceptionally large. conditions.text: Since the reform of last September, the exchange system of Colombia consists of three separate markets, two of them official and the third free. (a) The "preferential" official market is supplied by the receipts from coffee exports, in discharge of surrender liabilities calculated on the basis of an official export price which is adjusted periodically to conform roughly with the quotations for Colombian coffees in foreign markets, and exchange sales of foreign-owned petroleum companies for conversion into pesos needed by them to meet their local costs of production. This market is, in turn, available for selected import payments, mainly for imports of foods, drugs, and chemicals, and some official transfers, among them mainly some service paymer' s on the external public debt. (i) The buying rate for coffee export receipts is now Col$8.50 per U.S. dollar. This rate will not be depreciated by the Government in 1966, and the official surrender price for coffee export receipts will be maintained throughout 1966 at levels involving the fullest surrender of coffee export receipts that is feasible under conditions of fluctuating export prices. (ii) The foreign exchange sold by the petroleum companies is now converted for them at a rate of Col$7.67 per U.S. dollar. (iii) All payments through the preferential official market are subject to a rate of Col$9.00 per U.S. dollar. conditions.text: The Colombian authorities are determined to liberalize progressively the existing administrative exchange and import restrictions. The liberalization efforts will follow the following concrete lines: (a) All delays involved in the process of securing official exchange allocation, other than the compulsory waiting period of 20 days, will be removed by December 31, 1965, and no such restriction will be reintroduced during 1966. (b) At least 25 per cent of all imports by value, all of them subject to the exchange rate in the intermediate official market, will be freed from all quantitative licensing restrictions prior to January 1, 1966, and at least a further 25 per cent of all imports by value, again all of them subject to the exchange rate in the intermediate official market, will receive the same treatment prior to April 1, 1966. (c) The imports subject to the preferential official selling rate of exchange will not exceed 25 per cent of the total import value in the first three quarters of 1966 and will not exceed 15 per cent of the total import value effective from November 1, 1966. (d) The percentages of total import value referred to in subparagraphs (b) and (c) above should be understood as meaning fractions of total values of registrations of "reimbursable" imports. (e) The lifting of import licensing restrictions from any import commodity will be irreversible, except after prior consultation with and agreement by the Managing Director of the International Monetary Fund

conditions.text: In addition to the fiscal effects of the latest exchange reform, the Government has taken action to strengthen its revenue base and to observe maximum economy in its operating expenditures. The Government is prepared to take further action along these lines, if this should prove necessary in order to proceed with its investment program without any recourse to inflationary deficit financing. To preclude inflationary repercussions, the Government will limit its access to Banco de la Repuiblica in the manner explained in paragraph 10(a) below. To ensure the availability of noninflationary resources for its investment program, the Government will achieve in 1966 a current account budget surplus of at least Co$1.1,600 million, in accordance with the following schedule: a minimum cumulative Co1$250 million in the first quarter of 1966, a minimum cumulative Co1650 million in the first half of 1966, a minimum cumulative Col$1,250 million in the first three quarters of 1966, and a minimum Col$1,600 million in 1966 as a whole.

conditions.text: The restrictive effect of budget policy on demand will be strengthened by the credit policy. In order to ensure consistency of fiscal variables and the monetary and credit flows with the desired restoration of an approximate balance in the external accounts and the target for inflation, quarterly limits will be applied, as set out in annexed Table 1, to the total net domestic assets of the banking system and to the net claims on Government. This will allow for an adequate increase (40 per cent) of the banking system's claims on the nongovernment sector to finance the needs of expanding production. The local currency counterpart resulting from the sale of foreign exchange purchased under the proposed stand-by arrangement will not be available to the Government. The overall expansion of money plus quasi-money (34 per cent) resulting from these policies is expected to reduce considerably the ratio of broad money to GDP in 1979, which would be consistent with our forecast of a slight recovery of economic growth. This restrictive monetary policy will be continued in 1980.

conditions.text: Given the massive amount of payments due by Zaire on account of external debt service, an appropriate amount of debt relief must constitute a crucial element of any reasonable economic program. Zaire will seek to obtain a rescheduling of its medium- and long-term external debt under the auspices of the Paris Club and vis-a-vis the banks participating in the London Agreement with a view to bringing debt service payments to a reasonable proportion of export receipts. Also, with a view to limiting new increases in the external debt, new loans contracted or guaranteed by the Government with a maturity of 1-12 years will be limited to SDR 100 million during 1979 with the exception of refinancing loans contracted in the framework of the consolidation of the external debt and concessionary loans. Within this ceiling, a subceiling of SDR 40 million has been imposed on loans with a maturity of 1-5 years. With a view to managing effectively the external debt, the authorities have ensured that the necessary amount of local currency is set aside in the budget to enable the Office of Public Debt Management (OGEDEP) to meet all obligations on account of debt service. As regards the management of the foreign exchange component of debt service, the Bank of Zaire will assume the responsibility for the foreign exchange transfers, while OGEDEP will determine which public loans are to be serviced in conformity with the principle of nondiscriminatory treatment of creditors. conditions.text: The Executive Council is convinced that any further restrictive exchange or trade measures would run counter to the program's objective of reducing the rate of inflation in 1979 and 1980. On the contrary, Zaire will, to the extent feasible during the program period, reduce the degree of restrictiveness of its exchange and trade system with a view toward liberalizing all current external payments and transactions in the medium term. During the period of the proposed stand-by arrangement Zaire does not intend (a) to introduce any new multiple currency practices; (b) to impose new restrictions, or intensify existing ones, on payments and transfers for current international transactions nor to introduce new restrictions, or intensify existing ones, on imports for balance of payments reasons; and (c) to conclude new bilateral payments agreements with members of the International Monetary Fund.

conditions.text: A crucial requirement for Zaire's economic and financial recovery is the strengthening of its international competitiveness and the recovery of confidence at home and abroad in its financial system and management. The Zairian authorities recognize the need for a depreciation of the zaire that is substantial enough to re-establish the profitability of the export sector, in particular of Gecamines, to provide a needed boost to government revenues, and to narrow the wide gap between the official and the parallel market rate of the zaire. Effective Novemeber 1, 1978, the authorities have intitiated a policy of progressive adjustment of the exchange rate of the zaire. The monetary authorities intend to follow closely exchange rate developments and to make further changes in light of Zaire's economic situation and the relationship between the zaire and the major foreign currencies. Furthermore, in continuing this flexible exchange rate policy, the monetary authorities will be guided by, among other things, domestic price and wage developments and the need to encourage expansion in the export sector. Consultations with the International Monetary Fund on our exchange rate policy will be included in the reviews of the program prior to December 31, 1979 and June 30, 1980.

conditions.text: The National Bank of Congo will maintain a policy of strict control over credit in order to prevent a resurgence of inflationary pressure and to enable a gradual re-establishment of an equilibrium on the balance of payments without restrictions on current transactions. To this end, the amount of credit to the private sector, estimated at CF 16.5 billion at the end of June 1967, will be maintained within a ceiling of CF 20.0 billion during the second half of 1967. The ceiling on credit for the first half of 1968 will be established, in consultation with the International Monetary Fund, before the end of 1967. Moreover, no net increase in government indebtedness toward the banking system will be permitted during the stabilization period. Government indebtedness with the banks, net of Treasury deposits with the banking system, will not be allowed to exceed as of December 31, 1967, the amount reached on June 30, 1967 (about CF 92 billion). However, in order to enable the Government to meet its commitments under the budget once the reform has been initiated, bank advances, not exceeding CF 5 billion, may be granted. to the Treasury; these advances will have to be fully repaid by December 31, 1967 at the latest. The profit deriving from the revaluation of the net foreign exchange assets of banks will be used exclusively for the repayment of government indebtedness toward the banking system.

conditions.text: In the 1976 budget, the Government adopted several measures including increases in certain tax rates, to improve public finances. Nevertheless, as a result of a further decline in oil production, the overall deficit is still large. Hence, the Government intends to limit current expenditures with a view to bringing them in better balance with the longterm revenue prospects. The 1977 budget, now being drawn up, will limit total expenditures to CFAF 48.0 billion. Current expenditures, excluding debt service, will be limited to CFAF 43.0 billion, or at the level of expeaditures expected to be realized for 1976. Expenditures on wages and salaries will be held at the 1976 level, except for those in respect of hiring personnel completing their training. Transfers to state enterprises will also be held at their actual 1976 levels, pending the results of envisaged studies on improving their operations. Other expenditures, especially those for material and supplies, which have increased considerably since 1974, will be examined with a view to effecting the savings needed to keep current expenditures at the above-mentioned level. Capital expenditures will be for only those projects for which non-bank or foreign financing becomes available. In view of the high level of foreign debt service until 1980, the Government will as far as possible avoid any further increase in its short-term and medium-term external debt.

conditions.text: The rate of expansion in total domestic credit will be limited to 5 per cent in 1977; the level of domestic credit will not exceed CFAF 41 billion at the end of 1977. As credit to the Government is limited by the statutes of the Central Bank and as the present level is close to that ceiling, most of this credit will be extended for purposes other than the Government budget. Since commercial banks' liquidity has now been largely absorbed, they will have to finance a large part of their additional credit operations through rediscounting with the Central Bank. Thus, the Central Bank will be in a better position to control credit expansion; in order to limit total credit to CFAF 41 billion, the BEAC intends to limit its total rediscounts, including rediscounts of customs duty bills and advances to banks, to CFAF 12 billion at the end of 1977, compared to CFAF 8.4 billion at the end of August 1976. -5Trade and Payments Policies

conditions.text: The budget for 1962 was adopted by Congress in December 1961 and calls for expenditures equal to revenues at ¢ 422 million. On the basis of actual revenues in the first nine months of 1962, revenues for the year 4Attachment as a whole are now estimated at ¢ 360 million on the basis of existing legislation, and at ¢ 375 million considering legislation recently passed by Congress. On the other hand, certain expenditure items were not included in the budget and if only the absolute minimum of these are provided for there will be a further expenditure of a maximum of 0 28 million over the budgetary estimate. Taking into account the overestimate in revenues and the underestimate in expenditures a deficit of ¢ 75-90 million would emerge. However, the Government, through savings and can.cellation of expenditure authorizations, intends to limit total expenditures in 1962 to the budget level of 0 422 million in order to avoid aggravating further the fiscal situation. Over half of the probable deficit of ¢ 47-62 million has already been financed; the remainder is to be financed by a limited amount of borrowing from the Central Bank, approximately X 20 million, in anticipation of the utilization of foreign credit from the U.S. Government and a postponement of expenditures.

conditions.text: The budget for 1963 was submitted to Congress at the beginning of September and provides for expenditures equal to revenues at ¢ 442 million. The expenditure estimate includes ¢ 19.5 million for amortization of external debt and ¢ 13.4 million for the amortization of internal debt. The revenue estimate is based on the actual collection experience of existing taxes and Congressional approval of new taxes. Shortly after the present Administration took office in May 1962 it proposed a number of new tax measures to Congress. All of them have already been passed, including increased consumption taxes on gasoline, cigarettes, soft drinks, and beer, and a tax on commercial bank profits. Congress already passed a reform of the income tax whereby the existing partial pay-as-you-go system would be extended to all taxpayers and will discuss an increase in customs duties that would result from Congresst approval of Costa Rica's signing the Central American Integration Treaties. Accordingly, the Government does not intend to resort to the Central Bank for any net financing in 1963, but to finance temporary cash shortages. conditions.text: The policy of the Government to apply combined fiscal and monetary restraint is expected to re-establish domestic and external monetary balance in Ecuador. The Government is prepared, should the measures taken so far turn out to be insufficient, to take further measures. In particular, since the national budget for 1967 has only begun to be prepared, the Government wishes to review the position in consultation with the Fund no later than October 1966 in order to take what additional measures may be required to bring to full execution the program of policies that is described below. Considering the present very low level of the international reserves of the Central Bank, the Government of Ecuador, in carrying out this program, desires to insure itself of the support of the Fund. Accordingly, we hereby request a new stand-by arrangement for one year in the amount of $13 million, to be augmented by the amounts of any repurchases in respect of purchases under the requested stand-by arrangement. The Government of Ecuador will discuss with the Managing Director the currencies to be purchased from the Fund before making any purchase under the requested stand-by arrangement. We would suggest that the new stand-by arrangement take effect on July 15, 1966.

Dear Mr. Southard: 1.o Ecuador has continued -to pursue with remarkable success the stabilization policies initiated in mid-1961. The large deficit that was occurring in Ecuador's balance of payments at that time was first arrested and then reversed; considerable progress has been made toward stabilization of domestic prices; and Ecuador has resumed a satisfactory rate of economic growth. In 1962 Ecuador achieved an expansion in real income of about 5 per cent and the rise in domestic prices was less than 2 per cent, compared with an increase of 4 per cent in 1961. Whtile import payments in 1962 remained at about the same level as in 1961, the value of recorded exports increased 15 per cent. The consequent improvement on current account, together with an increased inflow of official capital, resulted in a balance of payments surplus that allowed a $12 million increase in Ecuador's net official international reserves. conditions.text: In the field of public finance, the Central Government and the other official entities will make every effort to finance themselves from noninflationary sources. With this objective, the Central Government will have to abstain from any new borrowing from the Central Bank; will proceed with all due speed with the implementation of tax reforms now under consideration; and will operate in 1962 under a genuinely balanced budget, - 11 - Attachment except insofar as a deficit can be financed with external loans. In any event, the combined amount of net indebtedness to the Central Bank of the Central Government and other official entities (i.e., the difference between the sum of the Central Bank's loans and investments and its deposits and related obligations in sucres to the Central Government and other official entities) will at no time during the period of the requested standby arrangement exceed S/ 250 million.

conditions.text: In recent years the dollar value of the Egyptian pound in the parallel market has been adjusted on a number of occasions. At the present time the parallel rate seems broadly appropriate. To achieve our objectives of rapidly expanding exports and encouraging workers' remittances, we intend to continue our policy of exchange rate flexibility. In determining whether exchange rate action is needed, we will be guided by developments with respect to price-sensitive exports, relative price trends in Egypt and abroad, and movements of the free market rate. Consultations with the Fund on exchange rate policy will be included in each review of the program.

conditions.text: Most of the structural reforms and specific fiscal measures we are intending to implement will affect the fiscal position only in 1979 and beyond. For the 1978 budget, we were unable to proceed with new measures, despite our earlier hopes. A sizable increase in total expenditure is budgeted, since although we have had some measure of success in limiting the growth of current expenditure, investment outlays are expected to rise sharply. The overall deficit in 1978 is projected at LE 1.9 billion, or LE 0.5 billion more than the outturn estimated for 1977. In part this increase is expected to be financed by greater foreign borrowing related to the investment program. Nevertheless, an increase in bank financing appears inevitable, with such financing expected to be LE 665 million in 1978, or 7.7 per cent of GDP. A continuation of present fiscal trends would result in a bank-financed deficit of some LE 1,050 million in 1979. Although LE 250 million of this increase represents the additional budgetary cost of exchange rate unification, and investment is projected to rise by LE 450 million, we recognize that a greater proportion of the rise in expenditure needs to be financed without recourse to bank borrowing. conditions.text: For these exchange system adjustments to have their desired impact on the allocation of resources, it is necessary that their impact be reflected in domestic prices, but we believe it is important for the success of the program that these effects occur gradually. The impact on the price level will be mitigated to a substantial extent by gains in efficiency and the elimination of scarcity profits at the distribution level, as well as by our general policy of fiscal and monetary restraint. Beyond that, however, we may apply a temporary export tax to potatoes to reduce the impact on domestic consumers and to capture part of the windfall gains already produced by high world potato prices. To partially offset the impact of the shift of imports of intermediate goods and raw materials to the parallel market, moreover, we have established a price adjustment fund to provide temporary subsidies for items particulary significant in the consumption of the lower-income groups. The fund is being administered in a flexible way. In general, public sector industries are expected to adjust their prices so as to cover the increase in costs resulting from the change in exchange rate and other factors. They are, however, free to apply for grants from the price adjustment fund to permit them to make smaller initial adjustments. conditions.text: In 1973 we formalized our previous system of incentive rates by establishing a parallel market which applied an exchange rate at a more depreciated level to a number of exchange transactions. Since that time we have progressively expanded the coverage of the parallel market, but even with this expansion the proportion of foreign exchange transactions occurring at the parallel rate has remained small. As a major step toward the establishment of a realistic exchange rate for the economy we have now sharply limited the range of convertible currency transactions to be carried out at the official rate. On the export side, only raw cotton, rice and petroleum and its products remain at that rate; thus to the exports already in the parallel market we have now added potatoes, fresh onions and garlic, cotton yarn and textiles, and cement. For imports only seven basic supply commodities--wheat, wheat flour, edible oils, sugar, tea, fertilizers, insecticides--as well as the noncapital imports of the petroleum sector, remain at the official rate. Last May we had moved a variety of capital and intermediate goods and raw materials to the parallel market; we have now completed the shift with the exceptions noted above. Most invisible receipts were already at the parallel rate; we have now shifted the remaining transactions, other than Suez Canal dues, to the parallel market. The ceilings for cotton financing after September 1, 1962 relate to the 1962/63 cotton season and are made on the assumption of a normal cotton crop. conditions.text: The Central Government budget for 1971, which is under preparation, estimates revenues at ¢ 320 million, or 11.5 per cent above the estimated level for 1970. The increase is chiefly due to the tax measures adopted in 1970 which will yield revenues on a full calendar year basis. Current expenditures are expected to amount to ¢ 274 million, as the Government foresees that some increases in wages and salaries will. have to be granted during the year. Moreover, maintenance outlays are expected to increase as a result of a more aggressive investment program. In the field of investment the Government is planning to push forward several new development programs in order to provide a stimulus to the economy by the expansion of public investment expenditures. The authorities are planning also to reduce further the level of the floating debt, therefore it is possible that some use of bank credit will be necessary during the period of the proposed stand-by arrangement. However, in order to prevent undue pressure upon bank resources, the net indebtedness of the Government to the Central Reserve Bank (defined as the sum of the Bank's advances and loans to the Government and its investment in government securities less its deposit liabilities to the Government) will not be permitted to exceed 0 34 million in the period ending October 31, 1971, and ¢ 37 million in the period of the stand-by arrangement remaining after October 31, 1971.

Consequently, the fiscal authorities intend to submit to the Legislative Assembly a package of tax measures with an estimated annual yield of over ¢ 30 million, or about 13 per cent of the expected revenue in 1967. On this basis and with the prospective growth in revenues resulting from a renewed drive to increase the yield of existing taxes through administrative improvements, government revenues are expected to reach 0 260 million in 1968. conditions.text: The budget approved for 1965 calls for expenditures, excluding debt amortization, of ¢ 242 million and estimates revenues at ¢ 216 million. Of the deficit of ¢ 26 million that has been budgeted, about ¢ 22 million is scheduled to be covered by net long-term foreign borrowing for development projects included in or supported by the budget. Further, the data for the first seven months of this year indicate that re enues in 1965 will exceed the original budget estimate, and under normal circumstances the Government would not have to resort to domestic bank credit to cover its budgetary needs. However, as a result of the earthquake, the Government is incurring emergency and reconstruction expenditures, and despite efforts to meet these new requirements through transfers from other budgetary allocations, total spending may end up higher than originally planned. Similar pressures will bear on the budget for 1966. Thus, the Government may have to resort to some financing from the Central Reserve Bank. In view of the credit needs of other sectors of the economy, however, it is the intention of the Government to restrict the increase in its indebtedness to the Central Reserve Bank to no more than ¢ 10 million above the level of ,16 million outstanding at the end of 1964.

conditions.text: Although the fiscal position of the Government has improved in the past two years, the situation is still somewhat tenuous. The cash deficit of the Government was reduced from 0 24 million in 1961 to 0 13 million in 1962. In 1963 the cash deficit is expected to be less than ¢ 10 million. Expenditures are to be limited to ¢ 189 million, as compared with the budgeted level of ¢ 192 million. Revenues based on the collection experience of the first five months of 1963 are estimated at slightly less than g 180 million. Congress has recently approved higher - 6 - Attachment import taxes on a list of luxury items (bringing these duty rates more in line with the rates established for the Central American Common Market), a tax on wheat flour, and production taxes on beer, soft drinks, and cosmetics. These higher rates of duty and new taxes are expected to yield a modest amount in 1963 and more in 1964. At the present time the amount of the cash deficit that will have to be financed through the Central Reserve Bank is uncertain, but it is the firm intention of the authorities not to increase the indebtedness of the Government to the Bank more than ¢ 6 million above the level of 0 24 million outstanding at the end of 1962.

conditions.text: For 1964, the Government expects the fiscal situation to improve further. In September 1963 the reform of the income tax is expected to be passed by Congress. conditions.text: Credit policy has been designed to provide the necessary support to the adjustment effort. In view of the very rapid credit expansion in recent years, in March 1978 the Central Bank instructed all banks to temporarily refrain from extending any loans or advances beyond the highest levels attained during the last quarter of 1977, and set strict penalties for noncompliance. Moreover, apart from highly exceptional cases, no increases will be granted in the banks' present rediscount facilities. The Central Bank also intends to make more effective use of other instruments of credit control, especially the prescribed ratio of nonrediscountable credits to deposits, and to activate as soon as possible the new statutory provision empowering the Bank to impose obligatory reserve requirements. In any event, total domestic credit (defined as claims on Government minus government deposits, plus claims on the private sector), which amounted to CFAF 171.1 billion at the end of 1977, will not exceed CFAF 176.0 billion during the period ending June 30, 1978, CFAF 177.0 billion during the period July 1-September 30, 1978, CFAF 178.0 billion during the period October 1-December 31, 1978, and CFAF 181.0 billion during the period January 1, 1979 through the expiration of the stand-by arrangement. conditions.clause: the limits on arrears in government payments referred to in paragraph 7 of the annexed letter are exceeded; or
conditions.text: The accumulation of arrears in government payments to foreign as well as domestic enterprises is a source of great concern. Although the claims of enterprises are still being reviewed by a technical commission, on the basis of the declarations of enterprises it is estimated that, as of December 31 1977, such arrears totaled CFAF 145.5 billion, equivalent to 56 per cent of the projected budgetary receipts for the current year. Conscious of the impact of these arrears not only on the financial structure of the enterprises concerned but also on confidence in general, the Government has developed a scheme for their consolidation and refinancing in the near future. Under this scheme, the Government intends to make cash settlements to enterprises of the order of CFAF 44 billion and to reschedule the remaining debt over a period of 8-10 years. Negotiations with the enterprises involved have already started and the rescheduling exercise is expected to be completed shortly. In the event that the amounts declared by enterprises are justified, the Government will liquidate all arrears no later than December 31, 1978. For this reason, adequate appropriations have been provided in the 1978 budget. In any case, the Government will ensure that the amount of outstanding arrears will not exceed CFAF 100 billion by September 30, 1978 and CFAF 60 billion by Decemlber 31, 1978. conditions.text: Apart from the consolidation and refinancing of the arrears, the Government has given urgent attention to resolving the broader issue of the deterioration of the public debt situation. In this regard, steps have already been taken to centralize the management of the public debt at the level of the Autonomous Amortization Fund. The latter will establish an exhaustive inventory of the disbursed and undisbursed public debt; set up a debt control and surveillance lechanism to monitor commitments, disbursements, and repayments of debt; and assume a key role in limiting new borrowing to amounts consistent with Gabon's debt servicing capacity. During the period ending December 31, 1978 new external borrowing by the Government or against government guarantee with a maturity of 1-15 years will be limited to CFAF 32 billion (SDR 112 million); within this ceiling, no more than CFAF 8 billion (SDR 28 million) will be contracted or guaranteed with a maturity of 1-5 years. The ceiling on new external borrowing for the period from January 1, 1979 through the expiration of the stand-by arrangement will be fixed during the discussions with the Fund staff as provided for in paragraph 10 below.

While the objective of the Government is to work toward the eventual abolition of import and exchange controls, any significant liberalisation will depend upon the availability of adequate foreign assistance to alleviate the present critical shortage of foreign exchange. Nonetheless, in operating the existing licensing system, the Government; will endeavour to be as liberal as is compatible with the country's balance of payments situation, and will ensure that the limited foreign exchange earnings of the country are utilised in accordance with carefully considered priorities. Commercial banks no longer have to refer to the Bank of Ghana before opening letters of credit in accordance with import licenses.
