conditions.text: The Bank of Guatemala's credit plan for 1972 is designed to be consistent with a small balance of payments deficit. In accordance with this objective,limits (which take account of seasonal variations) have been established on the net domestic assets of the Bank of Guatemala. These net domestic assets, defined as the equivalent of the currency issue less the net international reserves of the Bank of Guatemala, will not be permitted to exceed Q 10 million in the period ending August 31, 1972; and Q 23 million in the period of the stand-by arrangement remaining - 16 - Attachment after August 31, 1972. These ceilings will be reduced by the amount of any Treasury bills placed abroad as indicated in the last sentence of paragraph 5 of this letter.

conditions.clause: During any period of the stand-by arrangement in which the ceilings in paragraphs 3 and 5 of the annexed letter are not observed or the intention, in the last sentence of paragraph 7 of the annexed letter is not carried out
conditions.text: The authorities are determined to continue their policy of limiting the short- and medium-term foreign indebtedness of the public sector, in order to prevent this type of foreign debt from creating an excessive burden on the balance of payments. More specifically, they intend to reduce the public sector's outstanding short; and medium-term external debt.' Accordingly, the net foreign indebtedness of the public sector, with a maturity of less than ten years, will not be permitted to exceed the amount of $30 million during the period of the stand-by arrangement. For purposes of this limit, the public sector is defined to comprise the Central Government and its dependencies, the autonomous institutions, and the municipal governments. Within this limit, some borrowing will be necessary to refinance maturing credits, but these loans will carry maturities of at least five years. The Government may also find it necessary to place Treasury bills abroad in order to meet seasonal financing requirements, but for this purpose it is intended to issue only bills maturing within the same fiscal year. These Treasury bill placements will be outside the above-mentioned limit, but to the extent that they are effected, there will be a corresponding reduction in the limits on the net domestic assets of the Bank of Guatemala referred to in paragraph 3 of this letter.

conditions.text: Guatemala's financial plan for 1971 represents a continuation of the programs adopted in the past years. Although the net international reserve position of the banking system has improved substantially, the authorities feel that a further strengthening is required in order to assure the implementation of the recently adopted five-year development plan without endangering the financial stability of Guatemala. In order to achieve the balance of payments objectives, limits have been established on the net domestic assets of the Bank of Guatemala for the period of the proposed stand-by arrangement. For this purpose, the net domestic assets of the Bank of Guatemala are defined as the equivalent of the currency issue, less the net international reserves of the Bank of Guatemala. conditions.text: Consistent with the Government's stabilization policies, a monetary programme has been drawn up. As a key policy variable of this programme, limits have been established on the net domestic assets of the Bank of Guyana. These limits are set forth in the annexed Table 1. Moreover, limits on the net credit by the banking system to the public sector have been established consistent with the fiscal policy outlined in the preceding paragraphs. These limits are set forth in the annexed Table 2.

conditions.text: The Government considers it essential for the re-establishment of confidence that Guyana has traditionally enjoyed to eliminate as soon as possible the commercial arrears that have arisen during 1977. There was some reduction in these arrears during the first four months of 1978. In order to quantify precisely their level and to achieve their elimination in an orderly way, the Government of Guyana will introduce, by July 1, 1978, a system requiring that all requests for foreign exchange be accompanied by a local currency deposit of equivalent amount in a commercial bank and that, to the extent that a public sector enterprise or agency is not in a position to make the deposit, the Government will do so on its behalf; these deposits will carry a market-related interest rate. Furthermore, and so as to effectively sterilize the domestic liquidity accruing from these arrears, the Government will sterilize these local currency deposits referred to above in the Bank of Guyana, either through a legal reserve requirement of 100 per cent or equivalent measures. The Government is also determined to provide for an equitable treatment of foreign exchange requests. It is the Government's intention to achieve a further reduction in the amount of arrears outstanding over the programme period. To this end, limits on the total amounts outstanding have been established and are set forth in the annexed Table 3.

conditions.text: The deterioration in the internal savings performance during the past two years has led to a substantial reliance on external borrowing. Some of this borrowing has been at commercial terms and at rather short maturities. The debt service burden is expected to increase from 12 per cent of exports of goods and services in 1977 to 18 per cent in 1978 and 17 per cent in 1979. The authorities are actively seeking additional foreign assistance predominantly in the form of balance of payments support loans at concessional terms from international development institutions and the donors to the Caribbean Group for Cooperation in Economic Development. In order to prevent the debt service burden from prejudicing Guyana's future growth performance, the Government plans to keep the size and maturity structure of the external public sector debt under constant review and, specifically, to limit the contracting of such debt with an original maturity of 1 to 12 years to the amounts shown in the annexed Table 4. To this effect, the contracting of all foreign loans to the -8public sector and all loans with a public sector guarantee will continue to be subject to prior authorization by the Ministry of Finance. Also, the Ministry has taken steps to ensure that this authority is exercised effectively.

conditions.text: In addition to the reduction of arrears mentioned above, the Government is prepared to rescind the prohibition on transfers abroad of funds arising from depreciation allowances by foreign-based companies at an- early date, but in any case prior to October 31, 1978. Considering the extent of the existing disequilibrium, a further liberalization of the trade and payments system will not be possible during the programme period. However, should the current account of the balance of payments strengthen substantially more than is anticipated in the programme, the Government intends to further liberalize the system. Finally, during the period of the stand-by arrangement, the Government does not intend to introduce any multiple currency practice, impose new or intensify existing restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions, or impose new or intensify existing restrictions on imports for balance of payments reasons.

conditions.text: A relatively satisfactory growth rate is foreseen for all traditional export commodities in 1976, but prices of sugar will fall substantially below the level of 1975 and the price paid for bauxite-alumina exports and for rice will be only marginally higher than last year. However, taking into account the level of foreign borrowing now anticipated and the current holdings of gross international reserves (amounting to about four months of imports at the 1975 rate) the authorities have framed a financial program for 1976 which will permit a strong growth in imports while limiting the fall in net international reserves to at most G$100 million, which is roughly equivalent to the surplus of 1975. To this end, the net domestic assets of the Bank of Guyana, defined as the difference between the currency issue and the Bank's net international reserves, will be negative through June 30, 1976; will not exceed G$50 million through November 30, 1976; G$30 million through February 28, 1977; and G$60 million for the period of the stand-by arrangement after February 28, 1977.

conditions.text: As in the past, the operations of the public sector as a whole will be central to the attainment of the objectives of this year's financial program. With regard to the Central Government, the authorities are determined to limit total expenditure to the budget estimate. To supplement its own savings and provide for the increase in the level of development spending in 1976, the Government expects to make use of a substantial flow of foreign loans and of savings from the nonbank domestic sector, which will enable it to limit its recourse to net borrowing from local banks to G$124 million. The authorities anticipate, however, that the decentralized public sector will draw down in 1976 the substantial deposits accumulated in 1975 in anticipation of large capital expenditures this year. Consequently, the total net indebtedness of the public sector to the Bank of Guyana and the commercial banks will be held to the following limits: G$240 million through June 30, 1976; G$302 million through December 31, 1976; and G$350 million for the period of the stand-by arrangement after December 31, 1976.

conditions.text: In early 1974 the importation of a few consumer goods was banned or placed under quota and all imports were placed on licensing. With some exceptions, these controls have been administered flexibly, so that in practice their restrictiveness has been relatively minor from a balance of payments point of view. Also the Government of Guyana has traditionally maintained a unified exchange rate structure and a liberal exchange system for current transactions, except for a restriction on foreign exchange for tourist travel. However, in January 1974 the exchange allowances for tourist travel were suspended and foreign-based companies were requested to discontinue the exportation of depreciation allowances. These restrictions were intended to be temporary; consequently, in the light of the improvement in the balance of payments during the period, the Government of Guyana eased the restrictions on tourist travel in October 1975. Furthermore, during the period of the stand-by arrangement, Guyana will refrain from imposing new restrictions, and from intensifying existing ones, on current international payments or from establishing any multiple currency practice inconsistently with its obligations under the Fund's Articles of Agreement. During the period of the stand-by arrangement, Guyana does not expect to use import restrictions for balance of payments purposes.

conditions.text: The operations of the Central Government in 1974 will be crucial for the attainment of the financial programme's objectives. New taxes were introduced towards the end of last year with the budget for 1974. In response to the new situation additional tax measures have been introduced and a special sugar levy has been announced. In the case of this levy the necessary legislation will shortly be presented to Parliament. Also, emphasis will continue to be placed on improving the machinery for the collection and administration of taxes. On the side of expenditures, the Government recognizes that considerable austerity will need to be exercised. To this end, the Government has this year introduced measures to ensure stringent control over current expenditure (including public debt charges) so that these are not -5expected to exceed G$252 million in 1974; also, the Government is reviewing its capital expenditure programme to ensure that priority projects move forward at a reasonable pace, without prejudice to employment or financial stability. To supplement its own domestic efforts, the Government expects a higher level of project aid from external development agencies and will increase its use of medium-term funds from foreign banks. With regard to the latter, a loan agreement for the equivalent of about G$60 million will soon be arranged. In these circumstances, the Government expects to reduce its reliance on net domestic bank financing to G$25 million in the course of 1974. Taki

conditions.text: The Government of Guyana has traditionally maintained a unified exchange rate structure and a liberal exchange system for current transactions, except for a restriction on foreign exchange for tourist travel. In January 1974, the authorities adopted two temporary measures: the exchange allowances for tourist travel, which had previously been limited to G$666 per year, were suspended and foreign-based companies were requested to discontinue the exportation of depreciation allowances. The Government does not plan to rely on exchange restrictions on current account as an instrument of balance of payments adjustment; accordingly, it is the intention of the authorities to review the situation during the course of the stand-by arrangement, with a view to liberalizing the exchange system for current transactions. Meanwhile, the authorities request that the International Monetary Fund approve the present exchange system through May 1975. In any case, during the period of the stand-by arrangement Guyana will not introduce any multiple currency practice, discriminatory currency arrangement, or restriction on the making of payments and transfers for current international transactions inconsistent with the International Monetary Fund's Articles of Agreement and decisions.

conditions.text: In 1972 government current revenues rose by more than 20 per cent. This was partly due to large payments by the nationalized bauxite company following improvements in its financial situation, but also to a number of nonrecurrent factors such as the payment of company income tax due from previous years. Therefore, the performance of current revenues is not expected to be as strong in 1973. However, revenue should rise in line with the growth in the economy as the Government is determined to make further efforts to collect taxes in arrears and to ensure that tax and dividend obligations out of current income are paid promptly by private and public enterprises. This is not likely to lead to a strengthening of public savings, however, because a further step will be taken during 1972 to improve wage levels in the public service which have lagged behind those in the rest of the economy over the years. Nevertheless, the.Government intends to continue strengthening expenditure control procedures and it is planned that current expenditures, other than those related to debt service payments and the upgrading of civil service pay, will not increase by more than 8 per cent. conditions.text: The Government of Haiti has the firm intention of financing its operations in fiscal year 1962 solely from noninflationary sources. This objective will be achieved in the following manner: (a) Total budget appropriations for "fiscal" expenditures of the Government of Haiti will not exceed G 152.5 million in fiscal year 1962. Subject to paragraph (c) below, the Government of Haiti will limit total "fiscal" expenditures committed and paid to G 12.5 million per month. The remaining balance of G 2.5 million will be disbursed in October 1961 for a capital subscription payment to the Inter-American Development Bank. In view of the necessity of advancing the dates of salary payments to public employees due during the Christmas holidays, the G 12.5 million monthly limit for "fiscal" expenditures may be exceeded in December 1961 by an amount of not more than G 5.0 million, but any such excess will be applied against the monthly limit for January 1962. If in any month "fiscal" expenditures do not reach the above monthly limits, any amounts below these limits may be added to the limit for "fiscal" expenditures in successive months. To insure that "fiscal" expenditures are undertaken only if and to the extent that they are duly authorized and obligated, the controls of such expenditures at the commitment level are being strengthened, and special deposit accounts will be established in the National Bank for the separate handling of "fiscal" payments for (1) salaries; (2) pensions; (3) int

conditions.text: The monetary policy to be pursued in fiscal year 1962 together with the fiscal policy outlined in paragraph 7 is aimed at the strengthening of the balance of payments position and at the insuring of domestic price stability. These objectives are to be achieved in the following manner: (a) The aggregate amount of all outstanding National Bank credit (i.e., loans and investments, including the so-called "eligible portfolio" and other advances admissible for inclusion among the National Bank's legal currency cover) other than to the Government dealt with in paragraph 7 above, will at no time until June 30, 1962 exceed an amount of G 40 million and at no time thereafter until September 30, 1962 exceed an amount of G 32 million. It is the firm intention of the National Bank to direct credit availabilities within these limits to the greatest possible extent into productive lines. (b) The present statutory reserve requirements against the deposit obligations of private banks will not be lowered or otherwise altered and the regulations governing the distribution of their assets between holdings and investments in Haiti and abroad will not be changed in fiscal year 1962. Haiti has recently introduced legal penalties on reserve requirement deficiencies. These penalties and other effective controls will be promptly implemented if this should prove necessary to insure observance of these requirements and regulations. -7Attachment

conditions.text: The operations of the Central Government are of crucial importance, not only for the attainment of the objectives of the financial plan, but also because of their impact on public savings and the level of investment. The budget for 1972 estimates expenditures, excluding amortizations but including some extrabudgetary outlays, at L 246 million, or 9.3 per cent above the level of 1971. To finance this higher expenditure the Government submitted to Congress a comprehensive tax reform aimed at increasing substantially current revenues. However, Congress has not acted yet on the proposed tax reform, and although it has approved some other tax measures, the yield of these is somewhat difficult to estimate. The authorities are, therefore, determined to seek the speedy approval of the tax reform, aimed at raising the level of revenues; meanwhile, prompt action has been taken to revise downward the original expenditure appropriations. However, the authorities estimate that the Treasury will have to make some use of bank financing, although the amount will be smaller than in 1971. In order to prevent undue pressure upon bank resources, limits have been established on the net indebtedness of the Central Government to the total banking system. Accordingly, this indebtedness, which on December 31, 1971, amounted to L 69.7 million, will not be permitted to exceed L 68 million in the period ending July 31, 1972; L 81 million in the period August 1 through October 31, 1972; and L 87 million

conditions.text: In order to channel resources to selected sectors of the economy, the Government established last year the Agricultural and Industrial Development Fund, to be capitalized by the proceeds of the sale of bonds, transfers from the Central Government budget, and borrowing from abroad. The operations of the Agricultural and Industrial Development Fund have been segregated from the normal Central Government operations and the Fund will be used exclusively to extend credit to the private sector. It is envisaged that Central Bank net credit to the Central Government for the Agricultural and Industrial Development Fund which amounted to minus L 3.4 million at the end of 1971, will not exceed minus L 1.0 million until December 31, 1972. Honduras will consult the Fund and.reach an understanding on the ceiling for the period of the stand-by arrangement remaining after December 31, 1972. For the purpose of this ceiling, the Central Bank net credit to the Central Government for the Agricultural and Industrial Development Fund is defined as the Bank's investment in bonds for the capitalization of the Agricultural and Industrial Development Fund less its deposit liabilities to the Government for the Agricultural and Industrial Development Fund. -5 - Attachment

conditions.text: The Honduran authorities recognize that the domestic borrowing in 1968 will have to be kept within bounds that would avoid an excessive deterioration in the country's international reserves. Therefore, they plan to take measures, affecting both revenues and expenditures, that will limit recourse to domestic financing to an amount that reflects more closely the availability of bank credit resources and the prospects for placing bonds outside the banking system. With respect to revenues, the authorities have at present under active consideration a series of measures designed to increase the yields of the income tax, the property tax, excise taxes on luxury items, and the tax on gifts and inheritances, as well as a revision of public utility tariffs. On the basis of these studies, the Government plans to present a tax reform package to the Congress as early as possible during its ordinary session of 1968. Inasmuch as the global yield of the planned tax reform, and that part that could be made effective for the later months of 1968, cannot be determined with precision at the present time, the fiscal authorities are also preparing an expenditure economy program aimed at achieving substantial -5reductions from the amount budgeted in outlays not oriented towards the development effort. Furthermore, should investment expenditures to be financed domestically fall short of the budget target, the fiscal authorities will economize the resources freed to the full extent of the shortfall.

conditions.clause: the limits on Central Bank credit specified in paragraph 8 of this letter are exceeded, or
conditions.text: For the coming year, the credit program of the Central Bank is based upon the prospective real growth in the Bankts currency issue. This program is designed to allow for a further reduction in the Central Bank's net international reserves, but the fiscal and monetary authorities consider that the decrease in international reserves planned over 1968 is justified on the basis of the Government's program to achieve a breakthrough in the public investment effort in the coming year and its plan to bring about in 1968 a tax reform designed to raise public savings to a level adequate to support this development effort in succeeding years. To implement its credit plan, the Central Bank has established limits on total credit operations (currency issue plus the balance of any foreign loans to the Central Bank with a maturity of under five years less net international reserves) for 1968. These limits, which provide for the seasonal variation in credit requirements, are as follows: L 16 million in the first quarter; L 16 million in the second quarter; L 15 million in the third quarter; and L 24.6 million in the fourth quarter. Any foreign loans with a maturity of at least five years made to the Central Bank will, except for those credits used by the Central Bank to finance pre-investment studies, only be used to provide credit to the banks and development institutions for relending to the private sector.

conditions.text: The budget adopted for 1964 authorized expenditures of L 104.6 million, excluding amortization of debt, and estimated revenues at L 88.4 million. Net long-term borrowing from abroad for development projects included in the budget was projected to amount to L 12.7 million, leaving L 3.5 million to be financed from net domestic borrowing. The pace of tax collections in the first four months of 1964 indicates that revenues in the full year will turn out as originally estimated, and it is the firm intention of the Government to limit expenditures to the amount budgeted. The experience in recent years and in the early months of 1964 indicates that most of the projected internal deficit, of L 3.5 million, can be financed through sales of securities to the private sector, but a small part may have to be financed by the Central Bank. Thus, for the period of the requested stand-by arrangement, the limits placed on the net indebtedness (borrowing less amortization plus use of deposits) of the public sector to the Central Bank are slightly higher than those that prevailed in the corresponding periods of last year. A limit of L 13.75 million is to apply for the remainder of 19 64 until the end of November, when for seasonal reasons the limit will be increased to L 15.75 million. This L 15.75 million limit will then apply until the end of June 1965, when the net indebtedness of the public sector to the Central Bank will be reduced to a maximum of L 13.75 million.

conditions.text: For the period of the requested stand-by arrangement, the Central Bank of Honduras plans to follow credit policies designed to strengthen the financial position of the country while meeting the seasonal and productive credit requirements of the economy. In order to provide the Central Bank with more flexibility in its operations with the private banks, the limit on Central Bank rediscounts to such banks will be raised from the present level of L 3 million to L 3.5 million. This increased margin of credit will be used on a selective basis to stimulate an expansion in bank credit to agriculture and industry. Central Bank rediscounts to the National Development Bank are to be raised from the basic level of L 4 million established for the past year to L 4.5 million. An additional L 2 million in rediscounts will be available to the National Development Bank for seasonal financing of the harvesting and mobilization of domestic crops, the same seasonal accommodation as was provided last year. The rediscount limits established for the National Development Bank are L 5 million for the third quarter of 1964 and L 6.5 million for the last quarter of 1964 and the first half of 1965. These levels are (i) 27 per cent in cash and 15 per cent in securities against demand deposits and similar sight liabilities and (ii) 5 per cent in cash and 10 per cent in securities against savings and tine deposits and "specialized" savings accounts. -56. The fiscal and monetary authorities of Honduras believe the policies outlined above and the limited monetary expansion planned are in accord with the goals of defending the international reserve position of the country while maintaining the convertibility of the lempira and at the same time providing the growth of liquidity necessary for the growth (of liquidity necessary for the growth--sic) of the economy. Should these fiscal and credit measures not prove adequate in defending the international reserve position of Honduras, Honduras will consult with the Managing Director of the Fund, at his request, on the advisability of introducing additional measures to maintain external balance.

conditions.text: The Government's ultimate goal is, as mentioned above, to obtain an increase in Honduras' net international reserves. The Government, however, is also faced with the problem of an inadequate rate of economic growth in the past several years; for most of these years the rate of growth has been only slightly greater than the rate of population increase. This inadequate performance is mainly attributable to the weakened position in world markets of the country's main exports and, in particular, to the decline of the Honduran banana industry. Because of this situation, the Government intends to expand its efforts to accelerate the rate of growth of the economy; measures are currently under consideration which it is hoped will utilize more fully and effectively the domestic savings of the economy for productive purposes. Moreover, to compensate for the present deficiency of savings, the Government is actively seeking foreign financial assistance for its investment program. In this regard, the Government of Honduras intends to limit its use of external financial assistance to long-term loans for development purposes. As in the past, - 4 - Attachment the Government will not seek any short-term or medium-term external financial assistance, (i.e., credits of less than five years maturity), without consultation and agreement with the Managing Director of the Fund.

conditions.text: Monetary policy. During 1972, a source of credit expansion was the considerable increase in the foreign exchange liabilities of commercial banks. With a view to improving control of liabilities denominated in foreign exchange and partly offsetting the interest differentials between funds of domestic and foreign origin, Bank Indonesia announced on April 12, 1973 the establishment of a uniform reserve requirement of 30 per cent against such liabilities, including all advance import deposits, in place of the existing differential reserve requirements; at least one third of the required reserves will be held with Bank Indonesia and the remainder in cash in foreign currencies and in demand and call money deposits with correspondent banks abroad. The monetary policies that will be implemented by the Government during the period of the proposed stand-by arrangement - 25 will be appropriate to the attainment of its objectives stated in paragraph 3 above. Taking into account the credit and liquidity requirements of an expanding economy, on the one hand, and the need for cautious demand management after the recent price increases on the other, a phased ceiling has been established for'the net domestic assets of Bank Indonesia (gross domestic assets minus government and BUL deposits and the counterpart of foreign aid). conditions.text: It is the policy of the Government of Indonesia to limit, to the extent possible, borrowing from abroad by the public sector to long-term loans on favorable terms, taking into account the overall debt servicing capacity of the country. With this objective, a Presidential Decree concerning the contracting and approval of foreign borrowing was promulgated in October 1972; detailed regulations will be issued for the effective implementation of this Decree. Banks in Indonesia are not permitted to guarantee foreign loans contracted by the private sector. During the period of the stand-by arrangement, the Government intends to limit the amount of new foreign loans, whether from official or commercial sources, extended to, or guaranteed by, the Government and any public sector entity or guaranteed by Bank Indonesia that have initial maturities from 1 year up to and including 15 years. The amount of such loans authorized or contracted after March 31, 1973 will be limited to $220 million; within this total, the amount of such loans with initial maturities up to and including three years will not exceed $30 million. Total foreign borrowings of Bank Indonesia and the foreign exchange banks, which amounted to $31.7 million as of January 31, 1973, will not exceed $50 million during any period of the stand-by arrangement.

conditions.text: External sector. During the realignment of currencies in February 1973, Indonesia maintainedunchanged its exchange rate in terms of the U.S. dollar. This step was taken in order to strengthen the basic balance of payments position and avoid a speculative outflow of capital. Taking account of this adjustment of the exchange rate, the 1973/74 balance of - 26 payments is expected to be as follows. Net oil sector receipts are expected to increase substantially owing to higher prices and production, and nonoil exports are expected to be appreciably higher than in 1972/73. The expansion in economic activity is expected to lead to a substantial increase in non-oil sector imports, but the rate of increase would be lower than in 1972/73. Net official international reserves are expected to increase by $140 million in 1973/74. The Government of Indonesia will follow domestic and external policies aimed at achieving this improvement in international reserves. The establishment of a par value at an appropriate time is a policy objective of the Government of Indonesia. The Government will not introduce restrictions on the making of payments and transfers for current international transactions or multiple currency practices.

The rice program The Government of Indonesia continues to give high priority to increasing rice production, so that Indonesia may be self-sufficient in rice by the end of the Five-Year Plan in 1974. In addition to the official programs for providing credit facilities and agricultural' inputs, the operations of BUL are of great importance for attaining this objective. During 1971/72 BUL will continue to provide support for domestic producer prices of rice through its rice procurement program. At the same time, BUL will also be responsible for maintaining buffer stocks of rice in major consuming areas in order to prevent excessive increases in consumer prices of rice. It is the Government's policy that BUL should avoid incurring losses in its operations, and that bank credit should be used for buffer stock financing. conditions.text: (a) The Government of Indonesia will maintain strict controls over the contracting of external debt. The Ministerial Committee for Foreign Credits screens all applications for foreign credits made by government departments or agencies, state enterprises, and the private sector. The criteria for approval stipulate priorities and terms for repayment consistent with the present and prospective economic situation, and the debt profile of Indonesia. In general, it remains our objective (with the exceptions cited in the following paragraph) to restrict future external borrowings to long-term loans, on favorable terms, for stabilization and development. (b) Short-term trade and banking credits maturing in 12 months or less, and associated with the financing of current trade transactions, and medium-term credits of up to five years will be permitted only within an over-all ceiling on the outstanding amount equivalent to US$125 million. It will be our policy to permit medium-term credits only for the financing of priority projects that will lead to a speedy improvement in the balance of payments and on terms that allow for amortization in line with the expected increase in exports. Credits for the prefinancing of foreign assistance by governments will not be included in the above limit.

conditions.text: The Government of Indonesia will continue to follow policies designed to ensure that the expansion of money supply may not be excessive and that real cash balances will increase. In view of the rapidly changing price and monetary situation, it is difficult to forecast what degree of monetary expansion would be compatible with reasonable price stability and production requirements. Nevertheless to foster growth accompanied by relative stability in our economy during the coming year we have established a ceiling on the net domestic assets of Bank Indonesia (the sum of gross domestic assets including rice credits to BUL, minus liabilities on account of Government deposits, the counterpart of foreign assistance, and sundry accounts) which amounted to Rp 88.1 billion on January 29, 1969, so that they will not exceed Rp 126.5 billion on June 25, 1969, Rp 134.5 billion on September 24, 1969, and Rp 146.5 billion on March 4, 1970. The Government of Indonesia will continue to apply a -8selective credit policy, in order to channel credit mainly to priority productive sectors. Quarterly monetary budgets will be prepared indicating, inter alia, the expected expansion in credit to the various sectors of the economy, including credit for rice, and the expected increase in money supply.

conditions.text: The Government of Indonesia intends to pursue the objective of achieving a balanced budget in 1968, both in over-all terms and in relation to routine expenditures. Great care has been and will be exercised to ensure that all commitments, whether authorized or contingent, are reflected in the proposed level of routine expenditures. It is proposed to maintain cash salaries paid to civil servants and military personnel at the level sanctioned at the commencement of the year unless an improvement in the over-all budgetary position, especially in revenues, permits an increase. As for wages paid in kind, it is proposed to effect savings in the rations provided to non-civilian personnel, and to reduce the cost of food allowances by substituting cheaper grains for rice to the maximum extent possible. In order to implement the policy of a balanced budget, it is proposed to continue the practice of quarterly reviews, so that the authorization for each subsequent quarter will be determined in the light of the most current data on receipts. The Government of Indonesia is determined to meet its routine expenditures from receipts other than the counterpart of foreign assistance which are to be applied to the financing of the development budget and for financing production. To keep revenues abreast of price developments it is proposed to adjust their bases of valuation; in particular, it is expected to adjust the valuation rate for import duties and taxes in line with the BE market rate. conditions.text: (a) Since the middle of 1966, the Government of Indonesia has applied strict controls over the contracting of external debt. A ministerial Committee for Foreign Credits has been established to screen and approve all applications for foreign credits made by government departments or agencies, state enterprises and the private sector. The criteria for approval stipulate priorities and terms for repayment consistent with the present and prospective economic situation and the debt profile of Indonesia. In the case of government-to-government credits, excluding refinancing credits, the Government of Indonesia has obtained minimum grace periods of five years and repayment periods of at least 18 years at low effective interest rates. In general, it remains the objective of the authorities (with the exceptions cited in the following paragraph) to restrict future external borrowings to long-term loans for the stabilization, rehabilitation, and development of the economy at low rates of interest, and with grace periods which allow for the heavy burden of debt service during the next decade. (b) Short-term trade and banking credits maturing in 12 months or less and associated with the financing of current trade transactions (including credits under the "BE without cover" regulation) are to be permitted within an over-all limit on the outstanding amount equivalent to US$75 million. conditions.text: The Government's goal is to establish a par value as soon as possible. However, time is needed for the domestic price level to stabilize and for the balance of payments to improve, and to develop new tax measures which will produce revenues to replace those derived from the spread in the system of exchange rates. In the meantime, the Government will re-examine the operation of the present exchange system, with a view to improving it, and will remain in close touch with the Fund. No new exchange rates or multiple currency practices will be introduced, and the objective will be to gradually reduce the divergences among market rates, with a view to the eventual establishment of a unified foreign exchange market. While the authorities believe that the rate of inflation will be substantially reduced in 1968 as a result of government policies, it is recognized that prices are not likely to be stabilized quickly. It will, therefore, be necessary to follow a flexible exchange rate policy in line with changes in domestic prices. Accordingly, the exchange rates quoted by the Central Bank will follow fundamental market trends. The Central Bank will intervene as a seller only to smooth out fluctuations arising from temporary factors. As a guideline for the implementation of the exchange rate policy stated above, the net foreign exchange position of the monetary authorities will not be lower on December 31, 1968, than the level on December 31, 1967. conditions.text: As part of its new program, the Government has revised the system of exchange rates. Under the new system, the effective exchange rate of invisible receipts is Rp 315 and for exports, after taking account of the 5 per cent retention, is about Rp 350 per U.S. dollar. For exporters this represents an increase of almost 40 per cent in the nlpiah receipts from -4exchange earnings as compared with the export rates existing prior to May 27, 1963. The 10 per cent tax on exports has also been eliminated and automatic allocations of import licenses will be made equal to 10 per cent and 15 per cent of the value of exports for exporters and exporter-producers respectively. Bank Indonesia exchange sales will take place at three exchange rates: Rp 315 per U.S. dollar for Category I imports which includes chiefly rice, textiles, and medicines; Rp 540 for Category II imports which includes mainly raw materials and spare parts; and Rp 810 for less essential imports. These new rates involve a very substantial increase in costs for imports, especially for Category I imports.

conditions.text: Within the above framework of medium-term policies, the Government will formulate annual programmes, to coincide with fiscal years, with respect to specific objectives and policy'measures. During the preparation of each year's programme, its broad outlines will be discussed with the Managing Director. For the fiscal year 1975/76, policies will be geared to limiting the loss in Kenya's own exchange reserves to about SDR 26 million in calendar 1975 and to about SDR 12 million in calendar 1976. On present expectations exports of goods and services, in current market prices, will increase by 4 per cent in 1975 and 17 per cent in 1976. Imports of goods and services in current prices will increase by 4 per cent in 1975 but may decline somewhat in real terms, although the rate of growth in real GDP is anticipated to be about 5 per cent. Producer prices for the current crop season will be held at their present levels and progress will be made in the extension of agricultural credit; the AFC plans to decentralize further its lending operations to enable branch managers to authorize small loans and expects that an additional 15,00020,000 small holders should be receiving development credit from it during the next couple of years. The 1975/76 budget is at present under preparation and the Government plans to budget for a recurrent surplus equivalent to about 30 per cent of the anticipated development expenditure, which is to rise by about 25 per cent over the expected 1974/75 outturn. The overall deficit was W 236 billion, of which W 176 billion was in nonbudgetary accounts. The Central Bank financed W 191 billion of the overall deficit. Through the first quarter of 1975, stimulative fiscal action was continued in order to help sustain economic activity and employment. However, during the second quarter increasing fiscal restraint resulted in a pronounced contraction in net central bank credit to the Government. In the first half of the year receipts amounted to W 609 billion, and the current account registered a surplus of W 184 billion; however, capital expenditures of W 202 billion resulted in a budget deficit of W 18 billion. In spite of adaptations in the operations of the Grain Management Fund (GMF) increased costs resulted in a deficit of nonbudgetary account of W 138 billion, and the overall fiscal deficit was W 156 billion as of June 30, 1975, of which net central bank financing was W 145 billion. Interest rates on 3- and 6-month time deposits were increased by 2 to 3 per cent in December 1974, but this increase was partially reversed in July 1975. conditions.text: Fiscal performance deteriorated in 1972 owing partly to a reduced growth rate of tax revenues and partly due to an increase in expenditures, and a larger deficit in the nonbudgetary accounts, in particular, the Grain Management Fund. With a view to stimulating economic activity, tax reductions were introduced in early 1972 and again as a part of the August measures. Among others, the originally planned tariff reform including considerable reductions in exemptions on customs duties relating to export industries was postponed. Simultaneously expenditures were stepped up and outlays on public works advanced to provide the needed stimulus to the economy. In addition, the unusually large increase in grain stocks in 1972, also contributed in some measure to an increase in the budgetary deficit. A part of the overall deficit (W 45 billion) was financed by central bank credit, while W 88.7 billion was financed by foreign borrowings. conditions.text: Fiscal performance has remained generally satisfactory in 1970 and in the first nine months of 1971, and during the whole of 1971 the Government will again aim at a budgetary surplus or at least a balance on a cash basis. The achievement of this policy objective will be helped in part by rapid increases in tax revenues and by the continued restraint in current expenditures of the Government. The full operation of the Grain Management Fund, which was established in 1970 primarily with the sales proceeds of grain imports, is also expected to reduce budgetary expenditures for the Government's grain procurement. Furthermore, the Government has reviewed the existing tax system and submitted to the National Assembly a number of tax reform bills. Some of these are designed to reduce the - 29 existing tax inequities and distortions and are expected to be implemented by early 1972. With the help of these measures together with continued restraint on the increase of expenditures, the Government will seek to achieve a budget surplus or balance in 1972. conditions.text: The achievement of a surplus or at least a balance in the Government's over-all fiscal operations will remain a central element in financial policy. Fiscal performance has improved in 1970 due to expenditure restraints and to intensified tax collections. The Grain Management Fund, which was established in July 1970 for the purpose of handling the Government's grain procurement and sales, is expected to reduce the need to rely on financial assistance from the budget and the central bank for such operations. The Government has recently reviewed the present tax system, in particular the import tariff schedule, and plans to implement some tax reforms in 1971 with a view to securing more adequate tax revenue on the basis of more equitable distribution of tax incidence. With the help of these measures together with continued firm restraint on the increase of expenditures, the Government will seek to achieve a budget surplus or balance during 1971. However, seasonal fluctuations in revenues may necessitate occasional central bank financing to the Government. Net central bank credit to the Government at the end of each month will not be allowed to exceed the amount outstanding on September 30, 1970 (W 6.3 billion) by more than W 9.1 billion through April 30, 1971. Thereafter, it will be reduced to W 6.8 billion on June 30, 1971. The level thereafter will be determined in consultation with the Fund.

conditions.text: Supplementing the fiscal measures described above, the monetary policy of the Government for 1971 will be designed to achieve further progress toward stabilization. Adjustments in the exchange rate will take account of changes in - 5 the wholesale price index. In the implementation of this exchange rate policy, net foreign assets of the banking system on March 31, 1971 and on June 30, 1971 will not be allowed to decline by more than US$10 million from their level on October 31, 1970 of US$399.3 million. Any gain of exchange reserves through an increase in the principal of cash loans guaranteed by banks or the Government for the purpose of generating won funds will not be included in the changes in net foreign assets of the banking system as calculated for this purpose. The permitted changes in the net foreign assets of the banking system during the remaining period of the stand-by arrangement will be determined in consultation with the Fund, following the review of the exchange and trade system with the Fund staff in mid-1971.

conditions.text: The achievement of a surplus or at least a balance in the Government's over-all fiscal operations remains a central element in financial policy. Budget operations were balanced during the first half of 1969. However, the fiscal performance during the second half of 1969 was adversely affected by serious floods and the associated increases in relief and reconstruction expenditures coupled with delays in tax collections, and by the larger outlay on grain procurement as a result of the bumper fall crop of rice. As a result, it appears probable that for the year as a whole, the budget may have ended in a small deficit, despite countervailing measures which were taken to step up tax collection and to save on budgeted expenditures. The Government will seek to achieve a budget surplus or balance during 1970. The budget for 1970 approved by the National Assembly provides for a continued marked increase in tax revenues and for a reduced rate of increase in expenditures, particularly on capital formation. The Government's financial program for 1970 will provide for no net financing of the budget by the central bank for the year as a whole. In the first half of 1970, the net central bank credit to Government will not be allowed - 4 to exceed the amount outstanding on September 30, 1969 (W 6.5 billion) by more than W 5.0 billion up to June 30, 1970, and the level after June 30, 1970 will be determined in consultation with the Fund.

conditions.text: The Government adopted a number of short-term measures to counter the rapid increase in domestic liquidity in recent months, caused partly by the floods. Supplementing the fiscal measures referred to earlier, a tighter credit policy is being implemented. Strong efforts are being made to accelerate the collection of agricultural and fisheries credits, taking advantage of the good rice harvest. The monetary authorities are also taking steps to curtail the growth of central bank credit and to effect an early payment of the reserve requirement deficiencies of certain commercial banks. Total bank credit, which amounted to W 630.6 billion on September 30, 1969, will not be permitted to exceed W 776.9 billion up to June 30, 1970, and the level after June 30 will be determined in consultation with the Fund. Thereby the increase in bank credit during the 12-month period June 1969 to June 1970 will be limited to 40 per cent, compared with an increase of 65.1 per cent during the 12-month period June 1968 to June 1969.

conditions.text: In 1968, the balance of payments situation weakened due primarily to an increase in imports of 40 per cent induced by the rapid growth of domestic demand and to some extent by the large imports of foodgrains necessitated by the drought. Although exports increased by 49 per cent to $500 million, there was a widened trade deficit and consequent increase in foreign borrowing. In 1969, the Government intends to exert utmost efforts to reduce pressures on the balance of payments. Since August 1968, the exchange rate has depreciated from W 274.80 per U.S. dollar to W 282.80 on March 15, 1969. The present exchange system will be maintained as a means of evolution toward a realistic exchange rate and the establishment of an initial par value at an early date. Accordingly the authorities will not intervene in the exchange market against the basic trend of the exchange rate. The net foreign assets of the banking system amounted to $321 million on February 28, 1969; the latter amount was equivalent to about 2½ months' imports at the level of expected imports in 1969. It is intended that this net foreign reserve position should be improved somewhat, but the maintenance of an orderly exchange market may involve some temporary decline in the net foreign assets of the banking system. However, such assets will not be allowed to decline below $301 million during 1969.

The Government will complete during the period of the stand-by arrangement the program of liberalization initiated in 1965 in conjunction with the adoption of the fluctuating unitary exchange rate system. In this Context, the Government will seek, in mid-1967, legislation for making :-:,? extensive adjustments in the structure of tariffs and commodity taxes. It will also seek authorization to make, at its own discretion, adjustments in such rates in the light of changing conditions. When such legislation has been enacted, the Government will immediately eliminate all remaining quantitative restrictions on imports, except for those maintained for strictly noneconomic reasons. Moreover, the unspecified category will be completely -6eliminated. Prior to seeking the above legislation, the Government will, through administrative measures, liberalize the present system of import restrictions substantially. Toward this end, the Government will, by March 15, 1967, liberalize 73 items presently prohibited (about 20 per cent of total items prohibited) and some items in the semirestricted category by transferring them to the automatic-approval list. At the same time, 500 items will be transferred from the unspecified category, and most of these will be included in the automatic-approval list. During the remainder of the year, at least 1,500 additional items will be transferred from the unspecified category. In the course of 1967, the Government will review, in consultation with and at the request of the Managing Director, the progress made in implementing its policy of liberalization. The objective of existing controls on payments for invisibles is to prevent unauthorized capital transfers. Payments for most current invisibles, including profit remittances and repayments of principal on approved foreign investments, expenses associated with trade, banking charges, insurance premiums, etc., are freely licensed. Remaining restrictions on current payments for invisibles will be eliminated during the course of 1967. With the termination of the bilateral payments agreement with Japan on March 19, 1966, Korea does not have any bilateral payments agreement in operation. conditions.text: The Government of Korea has greatly appreciated the Fund's technical assistance in 1965 and its support of the stabilization program which have played a very important role by aiding the efforts of the Government to improve the economy. Since its introduction on March 22, 1965, the fluctuating exchange rate system has operated satisfactorily. After a depreciation of about G per cent in earlier months of the new system, the exchange rate remained stable at the rate of W 272-273 per US$1 in the following months. Restrictions on imports were relaxed considerably, and the restrictive system was simplified in 1965. Korea made further progress in 1965 toward achieving a viable economy. GNP at constant prices was estimated to have risen 'y about 8 per cent in 19C5, following an average annual rate of growth of 9 per cent in 1963-64. Industrial production expanded by 17 per cent, and over-all foodgrain production registered a record harvest. While foreign aid declined in 1965, capital formation was larger than a year earlier, reflecting sharp increases in domestic resource mobilization and in imports of capital goods financed with foreign loans. Exports in 1965 again rose by more than 40 per cent, imports by about 25 per cent, the deficit on current account was reduced and there was an increase in international reserves of $10 million. conditions.text: With the exchange reform, exchange certificates were issued for Korean exchange earnings from private sources and for a substantial portion of foreign aid. Exchange certificates were required for all private payments including most imports under the U.S. aid program but excluding for the time being imports under PL 480 arrangements. A free exchange certificate market was created and the Bank of Korea's intervention in the market was limited to maintaining an orderly market. The previous complex restrictive arrangements were simplified with the abolition of multiple currency practices. After liberalizing 75 per cent of Korean foreign exchange (KFX) financed imports at the time of the introduction of the fluctuating rate system, import liberalization was raised in subsequent months to 77 per cent during the last quarter of the year. -4

conditions.text: In the field of exchange rate management, the Mexican authorities have decided to seek the attainment of an appropriate value of the peso promising its greatest possible stability in line with normal market forces. This policy will be followed until it is possible to return to a fixed relationship with the U.S. dollar that is judged sustainable over the longer term. From now until then, the Bank of Mexico will intervene in the exchange market to prevent disorderly short-term fluctuations, while at the same time pursuing its balance of payments objectives with their consequential effects on its international reserves. Given the need to rebuild these reserves, the target for 1977 is an increase of the net international reserves of the Bank of Mexico by no less than the increase in its currency issue, both increases to be measured from their respective levels on December 31, 1976. The achievement of the aforementioned target will be verified each calendar quarter. For the purpose of this target, the net international reserves of the Bank of Mexico will be defined as the difference between (1) its holdings of gold and all claims on non-residents, but not silver, and (2) all its liabilities to non-residents, regardless of their currency denomination, excluding its obligations to international and regional financial institutions other than the International Monetary Fund. conditions.text: Although the budget for 1961, as approved by Congress, is ostensibly balanced, it does not include in the revenue estimates receipts from some new revenue measures introduced this year and some new investments that were deemed necessary. Last year the over-all cash deficit of the Federal Government was approximately Mex$600 million and was financed by the Bank of Mexico. Despite an increase in income tax receipts and increases in customs revenues resulting from a recent increase in tariff duties, it now appears that the Federal budget will be in deficit a similar amount in 1961. It is the firm intention of the Government to limit the increase in net financing of the expenditures of the Federal Government in 1961 by the Bank of Mexico to Mex$600 million. This deficit does include a part of the deficit of the public sector and is not considered inflationary, provided the rest of the public sector does not require a substantial net financing by the central banl, as it is equivalent to an increase of approximately 5 per cent in the total assets of the Bank of Mexico.

conditions.text: The credit policy of the Bank of Mexico has been to offset to the extent possible credit required by the public sector by sales of securities to the private sector, thereby limiting the increase in net indebtedness of the public sector to the Bank to noninflationary levels. The main instrument in this policy has been a comprehensive system of legal reserve requirements against deposit liabilities of both commercial banks and financial institutions (financieras). Through its sales of securities to the banks and the financial institutions to fulfill the reserve requirements, the Bank of Mexico has been able not only to offset most of the monetary impact of the deficits of the public sector, but at the same time has influenced importantly the direction of credit by the banking system. The Bank of Mexico will maintain the present level of legal reserve requirements for commercial banks and financial institutions. It will also continue existing regulations limiting the growth of short-term liabilities of financial institutions and of liquid liabilities of mortgage banks to approximately a maximum of 12 per cent per year.

conditions.text: Commercial banks will continue to hold with the Bank of Morocco deposits equivalent to at least 25 per cent of the increase in their total demand and time deposits and their external liabilities over their level of July 1, 1968. At the end of 1970, such blocked deposits amounted to about DH 100 million. While this measure has had the desired effect of mopping up excess liquidity and restraining the expansion of credit, its impact has been uneven as between different banks, with the required reserves varying between zero and 13 per cent of total deposits. This system does not appear consistent with the Government's efforts to increase private savings and channel them to the banking system. conditions.text: Our monetary program for 1978/79 provides for a slightly higher increase in the rate of monetary expansion than has been the case in the two previous years. Taking into account the projected real growth rate of the economy of 6.6 per cent and assuming an increase in the GDP deflator by 2 per cent, we project an increase in money broadly defined of 10 per cent. Based on the foregoing targets and projections and assuming a decline in net foreign assets of K 85 million, the expansion of domestic credit will amount to K 925 million (11 per cent) in 1978/79. Total domestic credit at March 31, 1978 is estimated at K 8,464 million. We will take measures to ensure that credit will not exceed K 8,850 million on or before June 30, 1978; thereafter, credit will not exceed K 8,990 million on or before November 30, 1978, and will not exceed K 9,389 million on or before March 31, 1979, and will not exceed K 9,466 million on or before June 30, 1979. Credit to the private sector is expected to grow substantially, reflecting increased credit to cooperatives that will be procuring larger amounts of agricultural commodities at higher prices, as well as credit to private sector firms and individuals. The Government has for a number of years been engaged in an effort to strengthen and expand the coverage of the banking system. This is being accomplished in part through recruitment and training as well as the opening of additional branches in areas outside of Rangoon. -7 IV. External Policies

conditions.text: The development of the Burmese economy will continue to require substantial foreign capital. An aid group under IBRD auspices has been formed to help ensure an increased and more coordinated flow of foreign capital. The Government is also prepared to consider foreign capital investment in certain export sectors, on a case-by-case basis, in the form of production-sharing arrangements and other forms of economic cooperation. Although Burma has no major foreign debt problem at present, it will seek mainly foreign long-term loans on concessional terms and avoid excessive recourse to foreign shortterm financing, in order to forestall a deterioration of the debt profile. To that end, the Government will limit total new contracting of foreign debts of the public sector with an original maturity of more than 1 year and up to 15 years to not more than SDR 65 million during the period of the stand-by arrangement. Of this amount, total new commitments with an original maturity of more than one year and up to five years will not exceed SDR 25 million.

conditions.text: Burma experienced relative price stability until about the middle of 1972, but prices have been accelerating since then, partly as the result of the crop failure in 1972/73 and the restrictive import policies that were pursued during the last two years. The consumer price index for Rangoon rose by 18 per cent during the period July 1972-June 1973 and by 30 per cent during the 12 months ended June 1974. The rise in prices was particularly rapid from April 1974 due to temporary rice distribution difficulties, and became a matter of increased concern. In June 1974, the Government initiated a program to reduce existing bottlenecks in the rice trade and to increase essential imports. As a result, rice prices have recently declined from their previously high levels while other prices have tended to stabilize. In the past, a major cause for the rise in prices has been the rapid monetary expansion. Domestic credit increased by 21 per cent in 1971/72 and by 23 per cent in 1972/73, mainly as the result of the increased financial needs of the public sector. The Government believes that, in order to contain domestic inflationary pressures, a better balance is needed between available real resources and the further expansion of domestic liquidity. conditions.text: The development of the Burmese economy will continue to require substantial reliance on foreign capital. In the past 18 months, relatively large amounts of loans with a maturity of less than five years were contracted in order to fulfill urgent import requirements, and the debt service ratio is expected to rise above 20 per cent again in FY 1975/76 due to sharply higher repayments of short-term loans. The Government realizes that continuation of this policy would impose an excessive debt servicing burden on the economy in the years immediately ahead, and it will strengthen its policy of screening new foreign borrowings and has already made institutional arrangements to centralize control of the contracting of external loans. In order to follow a cautious external debt management policy during the period of the stand-by arrangement, the Government will limit total contracting of foreign debts of the public sector with an original maturity of 1-15 years (excluding interest-free loans with a maturity of 10 years or more) to not more than US$35 million. Of this amount, the total of new commitments with an original maturity of 1-5 years will not exceed US$14 million. At the end -8of June 1974, the total outstanding external debt of the public sector was SDR 250 million, of which SDR 42.4 million had an original maturity of 1-5 years and SDR 95.2 million an original maturity of 5-15 years.

conditions.text: The operations of the central government are of crucial importance, not only for the attainment of the objectives of the financial plan but also because of the impact on public savings and the level of investment. Therefore, on the expenditure side the growth in current outlays will continue to be restrained. On the revenue side, continuing emphasis will be placed on improving the collection and administration of taxes. Moreover, some tax reforms, such as the use of the property cadastre for the assessment of the property tax, which have not been fully implemented in 1971, will be applied in 1972. The authorities intend also to review the tax structure in Nicaragua, but it is unlikely that these reforms will be adopted in 1972. In order to gauge the progress of the central government's current revenue, quarterly revenue performance targets have been set for 1972, as shown in the appended Table 1. With such a volume of expected revenue, supplemented by resources obtained through placement of bonds in the domestic market and by long-term foreign borrowing, the central government should finance its budget operations without any resort to central.bank accommodation, other than for seasonal-purposes.

conditions.text: In the fiscal field, the Government has been and is determined to reverse the downward trend in the ratio of tax revenue to gross national product that developed in recent years, in order to generate the public savings that are required to increase investment expenditure substantially, including transfers to the state development agencies, and to provide domestic matching funds for the use of available development loans from international agencies and foreign governments. Revenue measures have been or will be adopted and vigorous tax collection efforts are being made to achieve this objective. In May 1970 a single-stage, general sales tax of 5 per cent was established; the work on the real property cadastre is being carried on under an accelerated schedule and some benefits are being already obtained from it as the number of registered taxpayers has increased; modifications in the movable property tax, aimed at broadening the tax base, have been recently introduced, and a concerted effort is being made for the collection of other taxes. conditions.text: An essential element in the Government's financial program is its determination to strengthen the position of the National Bank. With the slower growth of economic activity since 1965 the National Bank has encountered increasing difficulty in mobilizing domestic savings while the relatively depressed condition of certain key sectors of the economy has hampered the recuperation of some of its outstanding loans. As a result the National Bank has become largely dependent on resources provided by the Central Bank and on the use of short-term and medium-term foreign credits. During 1968 the Government undertook an extensive reorganization of the National Bank and steps are being taken to introduce more cautious lending policies and to accelerate the recuperation of slow loans. In order to provide the necessary resources for the continued operation of the Bank, which plays an important part in the financing of the agricultural sector, the Government has negotiated a long-term external loan, the proceeds of which will be used to increase the Bank's capital, and has raised its own capital contributions. So as to ensure the availability of the domestic counterpart funds necessary for the use of this and other long-term external loans, the National Bank will require some additional credit from the Central Bank in 1969, but the amount of this financing will be strictly limited to an amount compatible with the over-all credit program of the Central Bank. conditions.text: The Central Bank of Nicaragua plans to continue following credit policies designed to strengthen the financial position of the country while meeting the seasonal and productive credit needs of the economy. Accordingly, the total domestic assets of the Central Bank will be limited to a maximum of C$220 million in the remainder of the first quarter of 1964. This total will then be reduced seasonally to a maximum of C$190 million in the second quarter of 1964 and C$165 million by the end of June 1964. conditions.text: It is the policy of the Government of Nicaragua to eliminate the system of advance import deposits. However, because releases of such deposits are similar to credit expansion in their impact on liquidity and foreign reserves, it will be necessary to move cautiously in this field. It is planned to reduce the advance import deposit requirements for items in List III from 100 per cent to 40 per cent in the coming year. IIowever, such requirements will not be reduced below 100 per cent before the end of April 1964, below 80 per cent before the end of September 1964, and below 60 per cent before the end of February 1965. The advance import deposit requirement for imports in List III will not be reduced below 40 per cent in the period of the requested stand-by arrangement after February 1965. The reductions in advance import deposit requirements have been phased over the coming year to permit the authorities to slow the process if they should find that the expansionary impact of the reduction is excessive. Advance import deposit requirements for imports in List II will be maintained at the current level of 40 per cent. The import categories covered by the advance import deposit system will not be altered during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement.

conditions.text: The National BanLk on its part intends to continue its cautious credit policy. In 1959 the Bank undertook to offset, by credit restraint in the private sector, the expansionary impact of the fiscal deficit. There was a tightening of agricultural lending policies by the Banking Department of the National Bank and the Issue Department of the Bank set an over-all rediscount ceiling for the second half of 1959 of C$175 million as compared with an actual level of C$224 million in rediscounts outstanding at the end of 1958. conditions.text: The credit policy of the National Bank specified in the financial program supported by the current stand-by arrangement brought an improvement in its liquidity position through the first seven months of 1969. From August onward, however, owing to the substantial short-term -6obligations assumed on behalf of the Government, the Bank's net reserve position has been declining, but this situation will be temporary. The authorities of the National Bank, in agreement with the Government, have decided not only to refrain from any further such borrowing, but also to relieve the National Bank from such obligations through the consolidation of short-term debts referred to in paragraph 5 above. Indeed, the Panamanian authorities are determined to re-establish a strong liquidity position of the Bank, so that it can play, in case of need, a stabilizing role in the Panamanian monetary system. These demands on the Bank were met by a reduction in its net international reserves, by financial assistance from the private banks operating in Panama, and by a reduction of the Bank's portfolio. In order to re-establish the liquidity position of the Bank, the authorities will reduce further the Bank's portfolio so long as the total of private sector deposits of the Bank have not recovered to the total of B 27.9 million of February 29, 1968. Moreover, a minimum of 20 per cent of any increase in the Bank's total private sector deposits beyond their present level of B 24.92 million and at least one half of any increase in these deposits beyond their February 29, 1968 level will be retained as additions to the Bank's net international reserves (including its holdings of foreign currency) during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement.

conditions.text: In the area of credit policy we have designed a monetary program which we believe to be consistent with our overall stabilization policy. As a key policy variable of this program we have established limits on the net domestic assets of the banking system. These limits, which are set forth in the annexed Table 1, will be reduced by any disbursements of general purpose foreign bank loans, program loans, and refinancing credits to the nonfinancial public sector. Moreover, in order to ensure that adequate resources are available to the private sector, we have established limits on the net credit of.,the banking system to the public sector. These limits, which are consistent with the fiscal policy outlined in the preceding paragraph, are set forth in the annexed Table 2; they also will be reduced by disbursements of general purpose foreign bank loans, program loans, and refinancing credits to the nonfinancial public sector. With a view to reversing the trend of declining real savings through the banking system, we raised interest rates on loans and deposits twice during 1976. Although at this writing the acceleration of inflation has rendered these rates negative once again, we are confident that the prompt control of credit expansion will lower the inflation rate and restore positive real interest rates. Should this not be the case, by the end of the first quarter of 1978 we shall increase interest rates unless it appears probable that the inflation rate will be significantly low

conditions.text: Of foremost importance to the furtherance of stabilization is the restoration of Peru's competitive position and the re-establishment of confidence. Effective October 11, 1977 the Central Reserve Bank of Peru freed the exchange rate for the sol, permitting its value to be determined to a maximum extent by market forces. This action was taken to provide the basis for a speedy restoration of balance of payments equilibrium and the re-establishment of confidence. During the program period, the banking system will intervene in the exchange market only to counteract erratic or seasonal movements and to provide for the progressive restoration of balance of payments equilibrium. This intervention policy will be geared to limiting the overall balance of payments deficit for 1978 to US$150 million, excluding disbursements of general purpose foreign bank loans, program loans, and refinancing credits. Quarterly targets consistent with this objective have been set for the net international reserve position of the banking system, as shown in Table 3.

conditions.text: The deterioration in internal savings performance over the last several years, coupled with our public investment effort, led to excessive reliance on external borrowing. With prices for Peru's exports below the levels we had projected, Peru faces service payments on external debt of more than one year amounting to 37 per cent of merchandise exports in 1977 and rising to approximately 48 per cent in 1979. Consequently, in order to prevent the debt service burden from prejudicing Peru's future growth performance, we plan to keep the size and maturity structure of the external debt under continuing review and, specifically, to limit the contracting of new public and publicly guaranteed external debt with an original maturity of one to ten years to the amounts shown in the annexed Table 4. It is also our policy to press for greater export growth; this too will reduce the debt service ratio. - 9 - Attachment

conditions.text: Concurrently with the return to a free exchange market, we abolished the existing import system and import exchange budget, leaving as the sole requirement for the purchase of exchange for private sector import payments the obtaining of an import license. Such a license is automatically granted for all imports appearing on the permitted import list and meeting the minimum financing requirements for imports. These presently amount to 180 days for all goods imported by the public and private sectors, except capital goods, which are subject to minimum financing requirements of one to five years. Import licenses and foreign exchange will be made available without delay for all bona fide imports on the permitted list which meet the minimum financing requirements. Furthermore, while the permitted list remains in effect, no items will be removed from it for balance of payments reasons. It is our intention to reduce the minimum financing requirements for imports to no more than 150 days prior to July 1, 1978, to no more than 120 days prior to January 1, 1979, and to no more than 90 days prior to July 1, 1979. It also is our intention not to introduce any new multiple currency practices or impose new or intensify existing restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions.
