conditions.text: The Government is determined to improve the standards for controlling the foreign indebtedness of the public sector and the giving of government guarantees to private borrowers from abroad. The requisite machinery has already been set up in the Council of External Transactions, and this machinery will be streamlined and improved by strengthening the staff function of the Council's Secretariat and the advisory role conferred upon the Central Reserve Bank. Moreover, effective immediately, the Council will not authorize the public sector, including the state banks, to incur any new foreign debt with an initial maturity of more than 180 days and less than 10 years, except for special credit arrangements for bulk purchases of agricultural products by the -8Government or public entities and for short- and medium-term lines of foreign credit to the state banks. The Council will authorize any such new foreign debts with initial maturities of at least 10 years and less than 15 years only within the cumulative semiannual amounts shown in the statistical appendix. The same restrictions will also apply to all new government guarantees for foreign debts of the private sector, and any government guarantees for such debts with initial maturities of at least 10 years and less than 15 years will count against the semiannual public debt ceilings set forth in the statistical appendix. conditions.text: The Government and the monetary authorities are certain that full implementation of the incomes, fiscal and credit policies described in the preceding paragraphs will provide all needed support for the present exchange rate of the sol. The two exchange markets will be reunified as quickly as conditions permit. However, the balance of payments is only now beginning to recover, and only after the successful implementation of the program described in this memorandum will it be known whether or not balance of payments equilibrium has been definitively restored. In these circumstances, the dual exchange market system needs to be retained for the time being as a precautionary measure. So long as this is the situation, the Central Reserve Bank will normally operate exclusively in the certificate market, and it will intervene in the draft market only to the extent that this is indicated for smoothing out purely temporary pressures in this market. In order to make sure that any such exceptional central bank intervention in the draft market does not counter fundamental trends, the Central Reserve Bank will at no time until the end of 1969 be a net seller in that market on a cumulative basis counting from August 1, 1968.

conditions.text: As regards prevailing exchange restrictions, which are maintained in the form of regulations requiring prior Central Bank authorization for foreign exchange sales for specified items, some progress toward liberalization has been made in recent years. This has consisted of a two-pronged policy of selectively shifting some of the affected items to the freely importable list, and of increasing foreign exchange authorizations for the still restricted items. Looking ahead, it is our intention to substantially phase out the use of exchange restrictions especially those which are maintained for industrial protection. conditions.text: The exchange rate of the peso at the FOREX (Foreign Exchange Trading Center) where all transactions between commercial banks take place is currently around l 6. 72 to a U.S. dollar, compared with P 6. 77 in early 1973. As a result of changes in the U.S. dollar's exchange rate with other currencies, the trade weighted exchange rate of the peso appreciated by 2 per cent during the same period. The Central Bank has intervened in the market so far to smooth out seasonal and other irregular movements and to build up reserves to a satisfactory level. In the light of the uncertainties in the international economic scene we consider it important to retain the present exchange rate system. We also believe that the present level of the exchange rate of the peso is generally appropriate to the medium-term balance of payments outlook, the need to promote nontraditional exports and to reduce restrictions on current payments. conditions.text: We have continued to give careful attention to the control of external debt. Total external debt rose by only $97 million in 1973 to $2, 013 million. Of the latter, 20 per cent was in maturities of up to 5 years, 57 per cent in maturities of 6 to 15 years, and 23 per cent in maturities of over 15 years; the corresponding figures at the end of 1971 were 30 per cent, 55 per cent, and 15 per cent respectively. The ratio of principal repayments and interest to earnings on current account declined to 18 per cent in 1973 and is expected to drop further to 14 per cent in 1974. In 1971 the ratio was 25 per cent. In line with our objective of improving the debt profile, while generating adequate foreign resources to support our growth target, we intend to limit final approvals of foreign borrowings by the private and public sectors with a maturity of 1 to 15 years during the period of the requested stand-by arrangement, to no more than $400 million. conditions.text: The Government's monetary policy will continue to be cautious. During the period of the requested stand-by arrangement, the ratio of required reserves against bank deposits will not be reduced by more than 2 percentage points, of which not more than one percentage point will be effective prior to August 20, 1971; also the proportion of legal reserves required in the form of cash a-d deposits with the Central Bank will not be reduced. Further, the present rediscount rates of the Central Bank will not be lowered. The net domestic assets of the Central Bank were P 3,531 million on January 15, 1971. These assets, adjusted for the change in the net foreign assets of commercial banks, will not be allowed to exceed P 3,706 million through August 20, 1971. The Central Bank's net credit to the public sector, which amounted to P 2,257 million on January 15, 1971, will not be allowed to exceed P 2,454 million through August 20, 1971, and Central Bank loans and advances to the Philippine National Bank, which were P 866 million on January 15, 1971, will not be allowed to exceed P 916 million through August 20, 1971. conditions.text: Following introduction of the free foreign exchange market and the fluctuating exchange rate, the peso depreciated from P 3.90 per US$1 to P 6.435 per US$1 by the end of September 1970, when the rate was stabilized by the action of the commercial banks. It is our intention that for the present the exchange rate should reflect the basic supply and demand conditions for foreign exchange; it remains our objective that a viable par value for the peso should be established as soon as feasible. Any intervention in the foreign exchange market by the Central Bank will be limited to help smooth short-run fluctuations. During the period of the stand-by arrangement, we intend to increase the net international reserves, exclusive of Central Bank temporary external borrowings to finance the Development Bank of the Philippines' servicing of its external loan guarantees on customers' accounts referred to in paragraph 7 below, which amounted to minus $22.9 million on December 31, 1970, by $45 million by December 31, 1971 and by $65 million by the end of the stand-by period. Moreover, we intend not to permit net international reserves to decline by more than $15 million below the level of December 31, 1970 at any time.

conditions.text: Following the sharp depreciation in the exchange rate, the Development Bank of the Philippines has encountered severe difficulty in raising the domestic resources necessary to service its external loan guarantees on customers' accounts. This problem is expected to be of a short duration. However, the amount of such external obligations maturing during the first half of 1971 is $96 million, inclusive of interest payments. It is our intention that the Central Bank should borrow up to $25 million to facilitate servicing the DBP's external obligations. We intend that the outstanding amount of such borrowings will not exceed $20 million after August 19, 1971, $10 million after October 31, 1971, and shall be fully redeemed by December 31, 1971.

conditions.text: As the foreign debt servicing burden for the next several years is expected to remain substantial, the Government will continue to control private as well as official foreign borrowings, particularly of short- and medium-term maturity. The authorities have improved the registration and management of foreign debts of all government institutions and private enterprises, and have setup guidelines with a view to avoiding any undue increase in foreign borrowings. The Congress has enacted a law limiting the debt service/ foreign exchange receipts ratio to 20 per cent. The Government will limit, during the period of the stand-by arrangement, new foreign borrowings approved for the private and public sectors with an initial maturity of one to fifteen years to not more than $300 million. Of this amount, new foreign borrowings with an initial maturity of one to five years will not exceed $60 million. conditions.text: Monetary policy is designed to contribute substantially to the prospective improvement in the external balance and to the containment of inflation. By the close of 1977, the rate of domestic credit expansion had reached 34.5 per cent of the initial money stock, substantially exceeding the rate of growth in the money stock itself, before moderating to 32 per cent in the year ending March 1978. On average, the money stock grew by 22 per cent in 1977 compared with a 33 per cent growth in nominal GDP, but is expected to be reduced to about 18 per cent against an anticipated growth in nominal GDP of -3about 27 per cent in the year to March 1979. Taking this into account along with the target for the balance of payments, net domestic credit of the banking system, the total of which amounted to Esc 654.0 billion on December 31, 1977, will not be permitted to exceed Esc 701.6 billion on or before June 30, 1978; Esc 738.6 billion on or before September 30, 1978; Esc 795.7 billion on or before December 31, 1978; and Esc 811.4 billion on or before March 31, 1979. The resulting increase in net domestic credit in the program year is estimated at about 23 per cent of money stock at the beginning of the period.

conditions.text: The authorities intend to take every precaution to ensure that these budget outturns are realized. The revenue effort will be supplemented as necessary to make up for any revenues lost as a result of the phasing out of the import surcharge referred to in paragraph 15 below. Furthermore, any revenues from existing taxes that may exceed budgeted amounts will be used to reduce the public sector deficit and not to finance additional expenditures. Finally, during the period of the stand-by arrangement, the use of government securities to discharge tax obligations will be limited to arrears in direct taxes prior to 1977, as presently permitted by law. Thus, after allowing for other sources -4of finance, the net claims of the banking system on the public sector, the total of which amounted to Esc 129.8 billion on December 31, 1977, will not be permitted to rise above Esc 143.8 billion on or before June 30, 1978; Esc 148.8 billion on or before September 30, 1978; Esc 166.8 billion on or before December 31, 1978; and Esc 183.8 billion on or before March 31, 1979.

conditions.text: All imports are effected on the basis of import bulletins, which for imports not subject to quantitative restrictions serve a statistical purpose and enable the importer to obtain the necessary foreign exchange. For imports subject to restrictions, the bulletin is equivalent to an import license. Import bulletins are normally issued without delay. However, in late 1977 the process of authorizing import bulletins was subject to some delays, partly in conjunction with the introduction of new administrative procedures. As a result, a backlog of applications has been built up and the Government is seeking, in cooperation with private sector importers, to devise means of eliminating this problem. Already, the Government decided on May 2, 1978, that thenceforth all applications for imports of raw materials and intermediate goods would be authorized automatically. It is the intention of the Government that this automatic procedure will be extended, no later than June 30, 1978, to all other categories of imports not subject to quantitative restrictions, and that by the same date, the backlog of import applications will have been fully eliminated.

conditions.text: The Government of Portugal abolished its import deposit requirement at the end of 1977, but still imposes an import surcharge of 30 per cent on the value of items covering about 29 per cent of total imports in 1976, and one of 60 per cent covering 2 per cent of 1976 imports. The 30 per cent surcharge will be phased out gradually: effective October 1, 1978 the rate will be reduced to 20 per cent; further to 10 per cent effective April 1, 1979; and fully abolished effective October 1, 1979. The 60 per cent import surcharge, applicable mostly to luxury goods, will be maintained temporarily, but the Government intends to study alternative domestic tax measures with a view to phasing it out beginning in 1979.

conditions.text: The Government establishes an annual foreign exchange budget for its own operations as well as foreign exchange budgets for the various state agencies in charge of monopoly imports of certain basic commodities, primarily foodstuffs. These budgets are, however, only indicative and the Government intends to amend these budgets from time to time so as to avoid restricting imports through rationing of foreign exchange. The Government of Portugal does not intend to introduce any multiple currency practices, or any new restrictions, or intensify existing ones, on payments and transfers for current international transactions, or to conclude any new bilateral payments agreements with the Fund members, or to introduce restrictions, or intensify existing ones on imports for balance of payments reasons.

conditions.text: Given the importance to Romania's development plans of imports from the convertible area, the level of outstanding convertible debt, and the low level of convertible reserves, special emphasis is given to trends in the trade account in convertible currency. Consistent with this, every effort is being made to increase the level of convertible exports and to ensure that convertible imports are used efficiently. In the program to improve the balance of payments after the floods of 1975, quarterly targets were established relating to the trade balance in convertible currencies and in the present circumstances it is believed that a similar procedure would help in monitoring trends in this important aspect of the balance of payments. Accordingly, targets have been set providing for a trade deficit in convertible currencies of not more than US$160 million for the first nine months of 1977 and a deficit of not more than US$90 million for the year as a whole.

Romania's position under bilateral payments agreements is expected to decline by the equivalent of more than US$250 million. With respect to short-term convertible debt, an increase is against the policy of recent years but as a temporary measure it is inevitable. conditions.text: Monetary developments in 1976 were in line with planned rates of growth of monetary aggregates. Thus, money supply increased by 14.2 per cent during the year compared with the forecast of 14.5 per cent and there was an increase of 14.0 per cent in domestic short-term credit compared with the forecast of 14.6 per cent. These rates of increase were somewhat greater than in 1975, reflecting the large increase in total output, including that in agriculture and increases in stocks, partly following the 1975 decline and partly as a result of the good harvest. In 1977, the planned increases in money supply and short-term credit, at 6.3 per cent and 6.6 per cent, respectively, are less than those in 1976. The smaller increases should assist in encouraging enterprises to manage their inventories, including those of imports, in the most efficient manner. The smaller rates of increase in 1977 also reflect the fact that the increase in agricultural output will be less than in 1976, since in that year output was very high. The planned increase in short-term credit of the banking system, which stood at lei 194 billion on December 31, 1976, means that the level will not exceed lei 207 billion on December 31, 1977. Consistent with the seasonal pattern, which normally shows increases in the first three quarters and a decline in the fourth quarter, it is planned that short-term credit of the banking system will not exceed lei 214.5 billion on September 30, 1977.

conditions.text: The damage done by the floods, especially in the export sector, has greatly affected the balance of payments, especially in convertible currencies. The immensity of the export loss will inevitably mean a substantial trade deficit in convertible currencies in 1975, although during 1976 the authorities plan for an improvement. At this stage, however, it is impossible to calculate with any accuracy the position in 1976; that will need to be done later this year when the full extent of the flood damage is more clear. In the meantime, it is intended that the deficit in trade account in convertible currencies be limited to SDR 125 million in 1975. For the current account the deficit is expected to be SDR 258 million. Nhen the picture for 1976 is clearer, the authorities propose setting quarterly targets for the trade balance in convertible currencies and for the level of convertible international reserves. With respect to the international reserves, the current target for the end of 1975 is that they not fall below SDR 140 million. - 14 - ATTACHMENT

conditions.text: The Government of Rwanda feels that only a stable currency can serve as the basis for balance of payments equilibrium and for steady and coordinated economic development. It undertakes to maintain the domestic -6assets of the banking system at a level which will ensure monetary stability, while taking into account the seasonal financing requirements of the public and private sectors. Public expenditure will be financed entirely by means of budgetary revenue and resources derived from foreign aid. Throughout 1967 the financing of public expenditure will involve no change in the level of the government debt to the banking system, excluding the Treasury deposits with the National Bank of Rwanda and the counterpart funds deriving from U.S. aid. To this end, the necessary measures will be taken so that the net claims of the banking system on the Government as defined above, which amounted to RF 867 million at the end of December 1966, shall not exceed RF 1,017 million before July 1, 1967; RF 917 million before October 1, 1967; and RF 867 million before January 1, 1968.

In 1967 the Bank will continue to follow the same policy, which will remain liberal for the financing of exports and will limit the financing of imports to a level compatible with the balance of payments objectives set out in paragraph 8 above. The National Bank of Rwanda will take appropriate measures so that banking system credit to the private sector, which amounted to RF 210 million at the end of December 1966 (including RF 56 million to finance coffee exports), shall not exceed RF 490 million before July 1, 1967; RF 640 million before October 1, 1967; and RF 210 million before January 1, 1968. The ceiling on credit from the banking system to the private sector at the end of December 1967 will be lowered by a corresponding amount if credits' for financing coffee exports at that date total less than RF 56 million.' conditions.text: Since financing of public expenditure must be effected entirely by means of fiscal revenues and resources derived from foreign aid, it must not entail, for the year 1966, subject to a seasonal financing as discussed below, any change in the level of indebtedness of the Treasury vis-a-vis the banking system, which anounted to RF 750 million at December 31, 1965. Temporary recourse to bank credit will be necessary, to deal with the Treasury deficit that is traditionally recorded in the first half of the year. This seasonal disequilibrium is due to the fact that the fiscal revenues are collected mainly during the second half, whereas public expenditure is spread evenly over the year. The Treasury deficit in the first half of 1966 is estimated at RF 150 million. Consequently, the total credits from the banking system to the public sector will not exceed RF 880 million before May 31, 1966 and RF 900 million before June 30, 1966. Repayment of these credits will take place during the second half of the year, so as to bring the total credits of the banking system to the public sector to a maximum level of RF 850 million at July 31, 1966, and RF 750 million at December 31, 1966. During the last quarter of 1966, the Rwandese authorities and the Fund staff will review the economic and financial situation with a view to establishing ceilings on credit to the public sector for the first quarter of 1967. -710. conditions.text: The over-all demand for credit by the private sector in Rwanda is subject to marked seasonal variations. In the coffee-marketing period (May-September), the demand for credit increases rapidly, offering the only private bank in Rwanda (the Commercial Bank) possibilities for full employment of its resources and obliging it to rediscount at the National Bank. Apart from this period, the demand for credit remains at low levels, allowing only partial utilization of the resources of the Commercial Bank, whose position, for this reason, remains liquid during most of the year. Considering the seasonal credit requirements and the need to avoid excessive pressures on the exchange reserves after the lifting of the exchange restrictions, the National Bank will apply a cautious policy with regard to credit to the private sector. This policy will be liberal for export credits and restrictive with regard to other kinds of credit. The National Bank has already signed an agreement with the "Caisse d'Epargne du Rwanda" (Savings Bank of Rwanda) to avoid a credit expansion, and the Commercial: Bank has adopted a restrictive policy at the request of the National Bank. Total credits to the private sector stood at RF 101 million at the end of December 1965. They may be increased to a maximum of RF 140 million in April 1966 to finance a stock of petroleum products, and be maintained at this level until the beginning of the coffee season. conditions.text: Since April 1979, we have taken steps to reduce the growth of credit to the private sector. Over the program period, monetary policy will aim at meeting the liquidity needs of the economy consistent with a 5 per cent rate of real growth, the maintenance of price inflation within reasonable limits and an improvement in the overall balance of payments from a deficit of about SDR 8 million during the 12-month period ended May 1979 to a surplus of approximately SDR 1.8 million during the program period. Given the very low level of our external reserves--at the end of May 1979 gross foreign reserves were equivalent to about three weeks of imports-our objective is to build up reserves to somewhat more comfortable levels. Achievement of these targets will require a tight credit program. It is therefore important that credit be allocated to those sectors where it will be most efficiently utilized for productive purposes. At the same time, there is a need to stimulate savings to permit banks to intermediate more effectively in the allocation of funds for investment. For these reasons, bank lending and deposit rates were raised by up to 2 percentage points effective July 1, 1979. conditions.text: The development of our economy will continue to require reliance on foreign capital. While we will continue to make efforts to increase the ' inflow of foreign long-term capital on concessional terms, we also intend to limit short- and medium-term foreign borrowing in order to avoid an undue : increase in Western Samoa's external debt servicing burden. Accordingly, our intention is to limit the contracting of new public and publiclyguaranteed foreign borrowing with maturities of 1 to 12 years to SDR 13 million. The bulk of these borrowings will consist of government-guaranteed ~ loans to public enterprises to finance commercial projects which will con"' tribute to the expansion of exports.

conditions.text: Spreads between buying and selling rates for all currencies quoted by the Bank of Western Samoa presently exceed 2 per cent, giving rise to a multiple currency practice. Our present policy is to keep the spreads to 2.5 per cent on a weighted average basis and to limit to a maximum of 3 per cent the spread for any one currency. The existing spreads arose as a result of an exchange levy which was introduced in August 1977 as a temporary revenue-raising measure. We have explored the possibility of replacing the exchange levy by other revenue measures, but under the prevailing budgetary circumstances, the Government has decided to maintain it for -7 the time being. However, we will continue to explore the possibility of reducing the spreads to 2 per cent and it is our intention to review the situation before the end of 1979. In April 1979, the foreign exchange allocation for imports was tightened. The total allocation for imports was reduced by 11 per cent for the second quarter over the first quarter, and three items on the free list were brought back into the controlled list. These three items represented about 5 per cent of total imports in 1978 and were selected because there are adequate local substitutes. These actions were taken as temporary measures to deal with the immediate balance of payments problem. conditions.text: The Government will conduct with the Fund a review of the program by January 31, 1980. At that time, developments affecting the - 8 implementation of the program, including the exchange policy, progress in the reduction of external arrears, and the results of the approach to the Paris Club to seek a rescheduling of Sierra Leone's existing repayment commitments on foreign debt to which reference is made in the last sentence of paragraph 4(d), will be assessed. In the light of this review, appropriate understandings will be reached with the Fund concerning any supporting modification of the program that may become necessary regarding the ceilings on total domestic credit, on net credit to the Government, on external debt, and on the schedule for a reduction of outstanding external arrears. In addition, the Government will conduct with the Fund a mid-term review of the program by April 15, 1980. At that time the Government's macro-economic policies, including the budgetary proposals for 1980/81 and the exchange policy and progress in the reduction of external arrears, will be reviewed. In the light of the mid-term review, understandings will be reached with the Fund for the remaining period of the stand-by arrangement beyond June 30, 1980 regarding the ceilings on total domestic credit, on net credit to the Government, and on external debt, as well as the schedule for a reduction of outstanding external arrears beyond March 31, 1980.

conditions.text: During 1970, the Somali Government will pursue monetary and credit policies aimed at accelerating economic development while limiting the size of the over-all balance of payments deficit. In view of these objectives, the Government intends to keep its net indebtedness to the Somali National Bank below the same limit in 1970 as in the preceding year, i.e., So.Sh. 64 million. However, if the disbursement of budgetary aid from Italy is delayed during 1970, the Government will be authorized to secure temporary advances from the Somali National Bank against the amount of such aid. In this event, the Government's indebtedness shall be limited to So.Sh. 68 million until the end of March, So.Sh. 72 million until the end of June, So.Sh. 76 million until the end of September, and So.Sh. 80 million until the end of December 1970. Such advances will be repaid immediately to the Somali National Bank upon receipt of this aid, and the indebtedness limit will be reduced accordingly. In calculating these limits on credit to the Government, any new loans and investments of the Somali National Bank made with the Somali shilling counterpart of specific foreign grants, or loans of a maturity of more than five years, and received by it for relending to the Somali economy, will be excluded.

conditions.text: In order to improve management of the Government's account with regard to its position with the Somali National Bank certain items which were previously included in the private sector will be included in the Government's accounts in 1967. These items are related to the purchase of 50 per cent of the shares of Societa Nazionale Agricola Industriale (SNAI). This purchase was made with a foreign loan and was channelled through the Somali National Bank; repayment to the Bank is an obligation of the Government. This change is only an accounting change, however, and will not entail an increase in credit to the Government financed by the Somali National Bank. The net indebtedness of the Government to the Somali National Bank (i.e., total loans and investments outstanding to the Government minus government deposits) in the 1966 stabilization program was limited to Sh.So. 24 million; with this accounting adjustment the indebtedness limit for the 1967 program will be Sh.So. 41 million.

The objective of the authorities is to consolidate the improvement in the balance of payments attained in' 1966 while assuring the maintenance of a liberal import and exchange system. To support this objective, the Somali National Bank's total loans, investments, and rediscounts to the private sector and commercial banks will be limited to a maximum of Sh.So. 103 million. This maximum, however, will not include the loan to the Government for the purchase of the SNAI shares nor the Somali National Bank's credit to ENCE (the state trading enterprise); both of these credits were formerly included as part of the private sector in the 1966 stabilization program. The loan to the Government for the purchase of the SNAI shares, as mentioned above, will be included in the limit on Government indebtedness to the Bank. ENCE's elimination from the private sector ceiling is to ensure that a planned expansion in credit to the private sector will be available to that sector. Total credit by the Somali National Bank to ENCE is to be limited to a maximum of Sh.So. 6 million during the period of the stand-by arrangement. The limit established for the private sector in the program for 1967 thus is actually Sh.So. 8 million higher than in the program for 1966. 7

conditions.text: Having regard to the large potential drain on gross official reserves in the period immediately ahead, and to the limited scope for selling gold in excess of current production on the private market or mobilizing additional resources on international financial markets to meet any such drain, the Government on July 21, 1976 announced that with effect from August 2, 1976 a temporary import deposit scheme would be introduced aimed primarily at strengthening confidence in the rand during a particularly difficult period. In terms of this scheme, importers will be required, when clearing imports through the customs authorities, to make a deposit equal to 20 per cent of the f.o.b. value of the goods imported. These deposits will bear no interest and will be repaid to the importer by the Reserve Bank six months after the date on which they were made. Certain categories of goods, principally mineral oils, state imports, and (where specifically authorized) essential capital goods required in connection with development projects, are to be exempted. It is the Government's firm intention to remove the scheme as soon as circumstances permit, and in any event not later than February 2, 1977. The Government intends not to introduce any multiple currency practices or restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions or impose new, or intensify existing, restrictions on imports for balance of payments purposes without prior consultation with the Fund.

conditions.text: The revised budget estimates for 1975/76 are showing a rise in government expenditure of 25 per cent compared with the budget outcome in 1974/75 while government revenue--unexpectedly reduced by lower. mining profits as the gold price declined--is now expected to rise by only 8 per cent. The deficit before borrowing in 1975/76 has been revised from the original estimate of R 1,284 million and is now estimated at R 1,680 mil lion, but none of the increase reflects policy changes. The 1976/77 Budget will be presented in March 1976. While the exact proposals have yet to be made, it is the intention that, in the absence of unexpected changes'in the economic climate, public expenditure will rise at a slower rate than in 1975/76 and that the budget deficit should not increase in real terms. The estimated deficit in 1975/76 is equivalent to 6 1/2 per cent of nominal GDP.

conditions.text: Official foreign indebtedness of Ceylon has increased at a fairly rapid pace in the last few years and amounted to $351.6 million at the end of December 1968. Of this total, $12.4 million had an original maturity of between one and five years. In view of the heavy interest and amortization payments falling due in the next few years, we intend not to enter into new contractual obligations with an original maturity of between one and five years of a total amount exceeding $3 million up to the end of December 1969. We are also fully aware of the dangers of contracting excessive amounts of medium-term foreign debts with an original maturity of more than five years. We intend therefore to restrain, in consultations with the IBRD, such borrowings so that future service payments will be commensurate with foreign exchange availabilities. -7

In order to relate the growth of money supply to the expected increase in real output (about 5-6 per cent), it is our intention to limit the increase in the Central Bank's net dcmestic assets over the level as of May 17, 1965 (Rs 1,388.9 million) to not more than Rs 105 million at any time during the period of the stand-by arrangement requested below. We believe that a reduction of the budget deficit as proposed for 1965/66, together with the restraint measures * Bank Rate increased to 5% effective 28th May, 1965. -6we are adopting with regard to credit to the private sector, would keep monetary expansion at a pace which would help restore reasonable monetary stability. conditions.text: Bank credit to the private sector has increased substantially in 1963 and 1964, the rates of increase in these two years having been 22 per cent and 16 per cent, respectively, and has continued to increase sharply in the first four months of 1965. In order to check the tempo of credit expansion, the Central Bank of Ceylon proposes to raise forthwith Bank Rate*from 4 per cent to 5 per cent. Besides, we intend to limit the expansion of commercial bank credit to the private sector to not more than Rs 55 million during the period of the stand-by arrangement requested below. The Central Bank intends to continue the present 38 per cent special marginal reserve requirement against demand deposits, in addition to the basic reserve requirement of 12 per cent against demand deposits and 5 per cent against time and savings deposits. The People's Bank, which is a relatively new bank, has thus far been exempt from any marginal reserve requirement. However, we now intend to apply tu the People's Bank such a requirement at a rate of not less than 25 per cent. Also, the Central Bank will continue to persuade commercial banks to take all precautions to avoid the extension of credit for speculative or consumption purposes.

conditions.text: In the exchange rate area, a major adjustment was undertaken during 1978, which should facilitate export growth over the medium term. As stated in my letter of May 30, 1978, we shall continue to aim at the establishment of a unitary rate for the Sudanese pound and we shall give consideration as to the appropriate time to simplify and rationalize our exchange rate structure. To further encourage inward remittances by Sudanese nationals working abroad, the Government has today adjusted the special incentive exchange rate for such remittances from US$1.75 per Sudanese pound to US$1.50 per Sudanese pound. Given the extreme scarcity of foreign exchange being experienced and the outlook for the balance of payments in the near future, we anticipate that the existing import restrictions will remain as an unavoidable feature of our system. However, we realize that it is vitally important that export growth should not be hampered as a result of rising costs. Therefore, close attention will be paid to exchange rate policy during the program period and in determining whether exchange rate action is necessary, attention will be paid to developments in exports and movements in relative prices between Sudan and other countries. We shall consult with the Fund on the need for adjustments in overall exchange rate policy in connection with the formulation of the annual programs for 1980/81 and 1981/82 and reach understandings that are considered necessary.

conditions.text: As indicated above, our balance of payments position has been weak for a number of years. As a result, our gross foreign reserves, including the currency cover of LSd 7 million, have fallen to LSd 9.7 million at the end of 1971 while our short- and medium-term liabilities are well in excess of this figure. As already communicated to you, following the general realignment of the major currencies in December 1971, the value of the Sudanese pound was kept unchanged in terms of the U.S. dollar at LSd 1 = US$2.87156. At the same time we have considered further measures to strengthen our balance of payments position by stimulating exports and restraining imports and have now taken the following steps effective March 11, 1972. As exports of cotton and gum arabic are proceeding well, no additional incentive is required for these products at this time. For all other foreign exchange receipts we are applying an exchange subsidy of 5.18 piastres per one U.S. dollar. Similarily, for all exchange payments, we are applying an exchange tax of the same amount. The existing effective rate for certain invisibles has been abolished and the existing import surcharge of 15 per cent has been reduced to 5 per cent. We shall keep the operation of the exchange system under close review and, if necessary, take further action in consultation with the Fund.

A review of economic developments and the budget for 1972/73 will be carried out with the Fund staff prior to end of June 1972 and on the basis of that review understandings will be reached with the Fund by July 31, 1972 with respect to limits on domestic credit for the July 1972-June 1973 period. For this purpose, net domestic assets of the banking system are defined as claims on the Government, public entities and the private sector, net of government deposits (including P.L. 480 funds), the deposits of the public entities, and net unclassified liabilities; moreover, the proceeds of any external borrowing by the Government and public entities with a maturity of three years or less and any use of the local currency counterpart of purchases. from the Fund will be included in the net domestic assets.

conditions.text: The serious balance of payments situation in the recent past has resulted in the accumulation of arrears with respect to current transactions which amounted to LSd 5 million on December 31, 1971. This amount is mainly with respect to past profits and dividends of airline and petroleum companies. It is the Government's policy to eliminate these arrears. To this end, it will enter into arrangements by June 30, 1972 with the concerned parties establishing an agreed schedule for such elimination. Moreover, it will be our policy to meet all current obligations promptly so that there is no accumulation of new arrears. Further, in view of the large increases in public external debt in recent years, we will strengthen our debt control machinery, especially with respect to short- and medium-term debt.

conditions.text: The objective of foreign exchange policy continues to be to achieve a fixed unitary rate at a level which will provide adequate incentives for exports and permit the elimination of restrictions on trade and current payments. As an intermediate stage, the Government established in January 1964 a limited parallel market in foreign exchange which applies to border trade in commodities other than major exports, to all invisible receipts and payments not related to trade, and to capital movements. In addition, settlement of outstanding arrears is being permitted through the parallel market. The aim is to reduce gradually the arrears without subjecting the exchange rate in the parallel market to undue pressure. Moreover, at a later date some imports of a luxury character may be switched to this market. Capital inflow is freely permitted through the parallel market. Capital outflow, however, will be subject to the approval of the Exchange Office, and existing restrictions on import and export of Syrian banknotes will also be maintained. The Exchange Office will not support the exchange rate in the parallel market by sales of foreign exchange. The differential official exchange rate introduced in May 1963 applying to some imports earlier financed through the free market has been eliminated.

conditions.text: Monetary developments during 1973 and 1974 were characterized by large increases in domestic credit associated with increased borrowing from the banking system by the Central Government and by the parastatal corporations. The ceiling on total bank credit that was established in September 1974 in connection with the first credit tranche drawing will probably be exceeded. For 1975/76 the implementation of a more realistic pricing policy should reduce markedly the need of the parastatal corporations and of private industries for bank financing. The Government's decision to reduce substantially its recourse to deficit financing will further constrain credit expansion. The Government will ensure that total net domestic credit, which amounted to T Sh 4,750 million as of March 31, 1975, and is estimated at T Sh 4,825 million at June 30, 1975, will not exceed T Sh 5,500 million during the period ending September 30, 1975 and will not exceed T Sh 5,700 million during the period ending December 31, 1975. The expansion of credit that is here provided for includes T Sh 600 million in seasonal finance for the purchase of agricultural products. This amount is somewhat greater than was used last year, reflecting the higher producer prices introduced in 1974, as well as some increase in volumes. The seasonal credit will be repaid in the -6first half of 1976. conditions.text: The adverse balance of payments developments of 1974 prompted the Government to tighten import licensing policies. The Government also reduced business travel allowances and suspended dividend remittances to nonresident shareholders, remittances by residents to relatives abroad and tourist allowances. In practice these measures have been administered -7flexibly and the Government intends to re-examine the need for them in the light of balance of payments developments. conditions.text: In recent years, Tanisia has endeavored to improve the structure of its foreign debt and to moderate its burden on the balance of payments. To this end, the Government has limited its recourse to suppliers' credits with maturities between 18 months and ten years inclusive. Since 1967, the outstanding foreign debt representing loans with maturities of ten years or less has thus declined in absolute terms. At the end of 1969, these loans will constitute about 28.0 per cent of the total foreign debt, against 40.0 per cent at the end of 1966. Moreover, the Central Bank has pursued a policy of inducing commercial banks to reduce their short-term foreign indebtedness, which declined by D 4.5 million during the first nine months of 1969 and which, at the end of September, stood at D 4.1 million. This reduction, however, did not affect the liquidity of commercialbanks, since their access to the Central Bank can be increased, within the framework of the ceiling, by the amount of any reduction in their short-term foreign indebtedness. The Government is convinced that the pursuit of sound foreign debt policies must remain an important objective of its economic strategy. conditions.text: The Government is very concerned about the inflation differentials that have arisen between Turkey and its main trading partners and their effect on Turkey's competitiveness. It is the understanding of the Government that the maintenance of Turkey's competitive position is of foremost importance in order to accelerate the increase of export and other foreign exchange earnings and thus enhance confidence in the Turkish currency. The Government will review the relevant arrangements essential to this matter before the end of November 1979 and again before the end of March 1980 and will on those occasions, reach such new understandings with the Fund as may be necessary. In the meantime, the Government requests the Fund's approval on a temporary basis for the multiple currency practices that are part of the new exchange arrangements as described in paragraph 22 above.

conditions.text: The Government has now introduced very substantial additional measures involving a major depreciation of the Turkish lira which can be expected to bring about a significant improvement in the international competitiveness of Turkish exports, render the domestic cost of imports more realistic, and accelerate the improvement in the balance of payments. The principal measure was to introduce a two-tier foreign exchange system. Effective June 12, 1979, sales and purchases of foreign exchange for imports, exports and re-exports of petroleum, petroleum products, and chemicals for the production of chemical fertilizer, as well as purchases of foreign exchange proceeds from the exports of agricultural products subject to official support prices, take place at a rate of LT 35.0 per US$1, while purchases and sales of foreign exchange for all other transactions take place at an exchange rate of LT 47.1 per US$1. The multiple rate previously existing for sales of foreign exchange for travel abroad has been effectively eliminated. Exporters of manufactures and mining products will continue to be permitted to retain 50 per cent of their export earnings to be used by themselves or transferred to other industrialists for providing inputs for export production. The Government has instructed the Central Bank to ensure henceforth that officially quoted exchange rates are adjusted whenever any cross rate deviates by more than 2 per cent from the rate in an established international market.

conditions.text: An essential element for the restoration of confidence is the repayment in an orderly way of arrears in respect of payments and transfers for all external transactions. During the period of the stand-by arrangement, the Government intends to observe the limits on outstanding arrears set out in the annexed Table 2. New arrears in respect of payments and transfers for current international transactions will be prevented. Arrangements have already been made, as mentioned above, with respect to overdue convertible Turkish lira deposits, third-party reimbursement claims, and arrears in respect of public and publicly guaranteed debts incurred before May 20, 1978. The remaining arrears which have largely been incurred before 1978 are estimated to have amounted to US$1,800 million at the end of May 1979. The Government has announced contingent upon the completion of the loan agreement with the banks a schedule for the payment of these arrears and also offers the option of settling these overdue claims in Turkish liras. The Government intends to have all arrears repaid in a nondiscriminatory way within a period of 7 years. The Government ensures that all deposits due from importers in respect of all arrears will be maintained in full. Observance of these intentions will be greatly facilitated by an early implementation of the OECD's Special Assistance Program.

conditions.text: In view of the very high debt service obligations in the near future reflecting the rapid accumulation of external debt before 1978, the Government intends to pursue cautious debt management policies in line with the debt servicing capacity of the economy. It intends to limit, during the period of the stand-by arrangement, the contracting of new public sector or government-guaranteed debt denominated in foreign currency (other than by the Central Bank, refinancing loans, or in the form of the Special Assistance Program under the auspices of the OECD) to an amount of not more than US$1,000 million, for such debt with an original maturity of less than ten years; of this amount such debt with an original maturity of less than five years will not exceed US$500 million.

The Government recognizes the need for a liberalization of the system of payments and transfers for current international transactions and will begin to liberalize following an improvement in the balance of payments position.

conditions.text: Consistent with the Government's overall stabilization policy, a monetary program has been drawn up. In order to prevent the re-emergence of excessive domestic demand pressures, the Government has established limits on net domestic assets of the Central Bank. Furthermore, in September 1977 the Government increased by 5 percentage points the effective rates of reserve requirements in respect to deposits with banks. In February 1978 liquidity ratios for banks were raised from an average rate of 10 to 15 per cent. However, the regulations were modified to enable the banks to fulfill their marginal reserve requirements by investing 10 per cent of the increase in bank deposits in government bonds. The Government intends in the first year of the stand-by period not to lower the effective reserve and liquidity requirements. In the first half of 1970 there was a considerable expansion of Central Bank credit, mainly to meet the needs of the Treasury during the period while the budget proposals were awaiting Parliamentary approval. There was also withdrawal of deposits from the banks brought about by political events in our area. This also required compensatory action by the Central Bank. However, this expansion was more than offset in terms of the impact on money supply by an increase of LT 2.1 billion in import deposits held by the Central Bank. There has been a marked shortage of bank liquidity, which my Government now desires to alleviate within the framework of its over-all stabilization program objectives. To insure the implementation of an appropriate monetary and credit policy in the remaining months of 1970, the expansion of Central Bank credit will be restrained within certain limits as follows: (i) total Central Bank credit, as defined in the Central Bank's weekly balance sheet (Reescompte et avances sur effets, Autres avances et Portefeuille-titres), which amounted to LT 13,057 million on December 27, 1969, will not exceed LT 15,796 million before December 26, 1970; (ii) total Central Bank credit to the banking system, which amounted to LT 5,117 million on December 27, 1969, will not exceed LT 6,500 million before December 26, 1970; (iii) the combined total of Central Bank advances to the Monopolies Administration, the Sugar Corporation and the Sumerbank, which amounted to LT 2,446 million on December 27, 1969, will not exceed an amount of LT 2,746 million before December 26, 1970; (iv) total Central Bank advances to TOPRAK to help finance its purchases of cereals will be limited to LT 1,300 million at any time during the stand-by period; (v) total Central Bank short-term advances to the Treasury, which amounted to LT 3,029 million on December 27, 1969, will not be permitted to increase above LT 4,439 million, the present legal ceiling, and will be lowered progressively to LT 3,750 million by December 5, 1970. During the last two months of the fiscal year, Central Bank short-term advances to the Treasury will be further reduced so that they do not exceed LT 3,000 million on February 27, 1971 compared with LT 3,893 million on February 28, 1970. A review of the economic situation will be carried out before December 31, 1970, by which time the Central Bank will have established credit ceilings for 1971.

The Government of Turkey believes that the policies set forth in this letter are adequate to achieve the objectives of its program but will take any further measures that may become necessary for this purpose. During the period of the stand-by arrangement Turkey will consult the Fund in accordance with the policies of the Fund on such consultations,and on the adoption of any measures that may be appropriate. These consultations may take place either at the initiative of Turkey or whenever the Managing Director requests consultations because any of the criteria set out in paragraph 11 have not been observed or because he considers that consultation on the program is desirable. After the period of the stand-by arrangement and while any Fund holdings of Turkish currency above the first credit tranche include currency resulting from purchases under the stand-by arrangement, Turkey will consult with the Fund from time to time, at the initiative of Turkey or at the request of the Managing Director, concerning the balance of payments policies of Turkey. conditions.text: My Government wishes to effect improvements in our exchange and trade systems so that, in conformity with our obligations under the Articles of Agreement of the Fund and our understandings under GATT, they serve better the development aspirations of the Turkish people. My Government therefore will conduct a comprehensive review of the trade and exchange arrangements now in force, with a view to simplifying the present trading arrangements and obtaining unification of the exchange rate structure. Before the end of 1969 we will consult with the Fund on the measures that need to be taken in this regard. In the meantime no additional multiple currency practice or new restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions will be introduced, and existing payments restrictions will not be intensified. Indeed, to the extent that the legal structure of Turkey permits, the authorities will, without delay, introduce appropriate measures for consolidating the present -7effective rate structure applied to invisible transactions and for simplifying the arrangements concerning tax refunds to exporters. I am happy to report that one bilateral payments arrangement with a Fund member has been terminated. Turkey now maintains only two such bilateral payments agreements with Fund members. No new agreements with Fund members will be entered into and the Government will terminate the remaining ones as soon as this becomes feasible.

conditions.text: To strengthen its internal procedures of financial management, my Government has decided to carry out quarterly reviews of the budgetary position. To ensure that the policy decisions emerging from these reviews shall be effectively implemented, all appropriations will be allocated to the various departments, economic enterprises and other public institutions on a three-monthly rather than on a six-monthly basis. If, at these three-monthly reviews, it appears that our expectations concerning revenue will not be met, budget expenditure will be reduced correspondingly. We realize that the International Monetary Fund will be interested in our efforts in this sphere and, therefore, the results of the budget reviews, and information on any action that has been taken in the light of the reviews, will be forwarded to you immediately on their completion. We will consult with the Fund on the whole performance of the budget before the end of 1969.

conditions.text: Turkey's international reserves remain at a low level, and now stand at US$25 million. Although we intend to maintain the expected volume of liberalized imports, and although we wish to conduct our trading relationships with a minimum of administrative interference, it must be recognized that our margins of safety are extremely narrow. Therefore, the Government of Turkey would again wish to rely on the support of the International Monetary Fund. Accordingly, we request a stand-by arrangement for one year, from July 1, 1969, in an amount of US$27 million, to be augmented by the amount of any repurchases in respect of purchases under the requested arrangement. Before making purchases under such a stand-by arrangernent, the Turkish Government will discuss with the Managing Director the particular currencies to be purchased from the Fund. Plrchases under the stand-by arrangement will not exceed the equivalent of US$10 million before December 15, 1969, US$17 million before March 31, 1970 and US$22 million before June 15, 1970. However, before making a request after December 1, 1969 for a purchase under the stand-by arrangement, the Government will consult with the Fund and reach understandings regarding the circumstances in which such further purchases may be made.

In order to achieve the objectives of monetary policy mentioned above, the monetary authorities have decided to strengthen their instruments of monetary control and to improve the institutional structure of the banking system. In addition, the Turkish Government recognizes that it will be necessary to reappraise the economic situation as a whole whenever Central Bank credit or commercial bank credit reach certain levels. Accordingly, the Government will review with the International Monetary Fund both the country's economic position and the appropriate policy measures it proposes to take under the circumstances, if, at any time before June 30, 1964, total Central Bank credit to the private sector reaches the amount of LT 1,750 million, or of LT 2,050 million at any time before December 31, 1964, or if at any time before June 30, 1964 total commercial bank credit exceeds the volume of such credit registered on December 31, 1963 by LT 800 million, or by LT 1,600 million at any time before December 31, 1964. Furthermore, it is the intention of the Turkish Government not to avail itself of the full amount of the Treasury's borrowing facilities at the Central Bank. Should such borrowing reach LT 500 million at any time during the fiscal year 1964, the Government will review with the International Monetary Fund the country's economic position and the appropriate policy measures it proposes to take under the circumstances. A similar review will be undertaken if the combined total of Central Bank advances of the Sumerbank, Sugar Company and Monopolies Administration reaches LT 300 million during the period March 1, 1964 to July 31, 1964, or LT 230 million, in any other month of 1964. Finally, the credit established by the Central Bank for the Soil Products Organization (TOPRAK) to help finance its purchases of domestically-grown cereals, will remain at LT 250 million, and Central Bank credit to the Meat and Fish Agency will continue to be granted under the conditions established for the 1962 and 1963 stand-by arrangements.

conditions.text: The purpose of this request is to support the policies that have been adopted by the Government of the United Kingdom to strengthen the balance of payments and create the conditions in which it will be possible to get both unemployment and domestic inflation down from their present unacceptable levels and keep them down. The stand-by arrangement will also help to repay external debt now falling due and assist in maintaining orderly conditions in the exchange market for sterling. The Government's objectives and policies, which I shall summarize below, have been set out in detail in recent policy pronouncements, including particularly the Prime Minister's speech to the House of Commons on 11 October 1976, my speeches to the House on 11 October and 30 November and my statement in the House this afternoon.

It continues to believe, however, that in current economic circumstances there may be cases where particular industries which are viable in the long-term are suffering serious injury as a result of increased imports. The Government has introduced certain temporary selective measures in a number of such cases and has stated that it is prepared to consider the further use of such measures where they may be justified in similar cases which may arise. It wili be the Government's policy to reduce such protective measures as soon as -9 circumstances permit. During the period of the stand-by arrangement, the Government does not intend to introduce any multiple currency practices or impose new or intensify existing restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions.

conditions.text: It is nowr clear that the public sector borrowing requirement in 1975/76 will be substantially higher than seemed likely at the time of my Budget last April. This reflects the deeper than foreseen recession and a re-assessment of the intensity of inflation at the start of the financial year. There has been no significant addition flowing from policy changes, nor is any such addition envisaged. The evidence available suggests that the public sector borrowing requirement in the present financial year might turn out to be as much as £12 billion. This can be expressed as equivalent to 12 1/2-13 per cent of national income (measured at factor cost), and is on the U.K. definition of the PSBR, which includes the financing of the investment expenditures of local authorities, of the nationalised industries, and of other public utilities. The speed and timing of the reduction of the PSBR to meet the medium-term objectives must be related to the recovery of the economy, in response to the recovery of world trade. Although I have had to conclude that the present unemployment situation leaves little room for cutting the PSBR in 1976/77, it is my intention to restrain domestic demand in order to ensure that resources are available for net exports. In the absence of an unexpected change in the timing and strength of economic recovery, this implies a PSBR in money terms in 1976/77 of no more than the level now expected for 1975/76, representing a fall to around 11 per cent of national income

conditions.text: As was stated in my Budget speech, and reiterated in the WTite Paper on "The Attack on Inflation", it is essential that our policies should not be undermined by excessive rmonetary expansion. This remains my firm intention. In the first half of 1975/76 cyclical factors depressed the demand for credit and money supply increased at an annual rate of little over 10 per cent. Some recovery in the demand for credit -6seems likely from now on, and the authorities have already taken initial action to control the consequent expansion of the monetary aggregates. Present policies would imply domestic credit expansion at an annual rate of £9 billion in the second half of this financial year and in 1976/77. I am ready to make further use of the monetary instruments available, as and when events make this necessary, in order to ensure that monetary policy continues to support the achievement of the Government's overall economic policy objectives.

conditions.text: The Government remains opposed to restrictions on trade, especially generalized restrictions. However, in current-economic circumstances, there may be cases where particular industries which are viable in the long term are suffering or are threatened with serious injury as a result of increased imports and where the Government may need to consider temporary protective measures. For reasons of this kind, the Government announced on December 17 certain minor temporary restrictions on imports. If further measures of this nature were proposed, the Government would consult with the Fund. It is the firm intention of the Government not to introduce any multiple currency practices on payments and transfers for current international transactions.

conditions.text: The Government's fiscal plans for 1972 comprise two parts. First, a series of immediate steps have been taken to control expenditures and increase revenue, and further tax measures are planned in the next few weeks to finance the forthcoming increase in public sector wages. Secondly, a basic tax reform is being prepared which is expected to increase the equity of the tax system and strengthen the revenue base of the Treasury. This basic reform, which will be submitted to Parliament together with the General Budget, will require Parliamentary approval and therefore is not expected to be completed until the final quarter of this year. The approval of this reform will lay the basis for a substantial improvement in the financial position of the Treasury in 1973. With regard to the rates of the state agencies, the authorities also intend to maintain the realistic rate policy initiated in March and will adjust the rates in line with increases in costs. As a result of these measures, the Treasury deficit in 1972 is expected to be reduced to Ur$30. 6 billion, compared with Ur$41. 6 billion in 1971. Also, it is the intention of the authorities to limit credit to the Treasury from the monetary authorities to Ur$27.4 billion in 1972, or only about two thirds the amount granted last year. Allowing for seasonal variations in revenue and expenditure, net credit of the monetary authorities to the Treasury, which was Ur$54.9 billion on Derember 31, 1971 and Ur$6 9.7 billion on March 31, 1972

conditions.text: The credit plan of the monetary authorities for 1972 is designed to be compatible with the plan to reduce the rate of domestic inflation to around 45 per cent, while limiting the decline in net foreign assets of the monetary authorities to $6 million. Credit to the _5 _ Attachment Government will be substanitally less than last year, and bank loans to the private sector also will rise at a more moderate rate. The legal reserve requirements of the commercial banks, which were lowered in February, will be increased in June to the previous level. In line with this program, net domestic assets of the monetary authorities (defined as currency issue outside the monetary authorities plus sight deposits of the Bank of the Republic less the net foreign assets), which were Ur$122.1 billion on December 31, 1971 and Ur$134 .2 billion on March 31, 1972, will not exceed Ur$14 8.9 billion at the end of any month during the third quarter of 1972; and Ur$16 1.4 billion at the end of any month during the fourth quarter of 1972. In this effort the Central Bank will be assisted by the equivalent of SDR 17.25 million purchased from the Fund in May 1972 under the compensatory financing facility, as well as the resources available under the requested stand-by arrangement, and also substantial funds anticipated from other sources. conditions.text: As was indicated above, it is planned to limit the internal budget deficit (over-all deficit less drawings against long-term foreign credits) to Ur$3 billion in 1968, with cumulative quarterly limits as shown in annexed Table 1. During the year, if the trends indicate that the deficit will rise above the limits that have been specified, either because of a shortfall in revenues or a rise in expenditures above the level programed, the Government will act promptly to correct the situation. As has already -7 been noted, great importance is attached to attaining a level of ordinary revenues of at least Ur$30 billion in 1968, and therefore an important indicator of the need for additional fiscal action will be the trend in such receipts. In executing the fiscal plan for 1968, the authorities do not intend to allow lags to develop in the payment of salaries because of their serious repercussions on the economic position of public employees, and because the alleviation of inflationary pressures from such delays is only short-lived and hampers orderly fiscal and monetary management. In the same vein, the Government will try to avoid a reduction in investment expenditures financed from domestic resources below the amount contemplated in the budget. Moreover, it will make every effort to mobilize as promptly as possible development credits from external sources.

conditions.text: It is the firm intention of the Uruguayan authorities to pursue policies designed to strengthen the balance of payments performance so as to enable Uruguay to discharge its foreign obligations while maintaining a level of imports adequate for its economic progress. The authorities are giving a high priority to the repayment of the indebtedness incurred during the past two years on account of delays in import and other payments. They are determined to adhere to the schedule of repayments of such debts which was worked out in December 1965 and will pursue policies that will assure the nonrecurrence of arrears in the future. It is planned to effect the repayment;of foreign obligations to a considerable extent out of a surplus from trade and other current balance of payments transactions. In addition, there will probably be a temporary reduction in the international reserves of the Bank of the Republic and a use of such external credit facilities as may become available to Uruguay, including those of the Fund. The Government's policies will be directed to assure that the net international reserve position of the Bank of the Republic will, as a minimum, improve by US$17 million during the period of the stand-by arrangement. Some seasonal decline in the reserve position must be expected during the second half of 1966 followed by an improvement in the subsequent export season. Specifically, the net international reserve position will not deteriorate from its level of March 31, 1966

The limit will be Ur$10, 8 25 million at all times during the period ending December 31, 1966 and Ur$10,925 million at all times during the remaining period of the stand-by arrangement. Credits financed from foreign loans of at least five years maturity and channeled through the Bank of the Republic will be excluded from this limit.

However, on the strength of revised revenue estimates based on the collection experience of the first quarter of this year, and taking account of certain other adjustments in the revenue and expenditure forecasts, the estimated deficit has been brought down to roughly Ur$1,000 million. The Government recognizes that financing by the Bank of the Republic in this amount would not be compatible with the stabilization program. Accordingly) all possible measures will be taken to further limit the deficit. iIMost public service tariffs and the prices of some subsidized consumer goods have been increased substantially in recent months. conditions.text: It is the firm intention of the Government to reduce cash expenditures in the second half of fiscal year 1959-60 substantially below the Bs 3,350, i.e. a monthly average of Bs 558 million, expended in the first half of fiscal 1959-60. Total cash expenditures, which were Bs 389 million in January and Bs 360 million in February, 1960, will no event be permitted to exceed Bs 2,188 million for the period of March through June, 1960, including the repayment of Bs 308 million of short term Treasury notes maturing in this period and a payment of Bs 80 million to augment the resources of the Banco Agricola y Pecuario, or Bs 1,800 million excluding these two separate payments. Therefore, actual monthly cash expenditures, excluding these two separate payments, will be limited to an average of Bs 450 million for the period from March through June, 1960 and in no event be permitted to exceed Bs 475 million, in any one month. Cash revenues are currently estimated at Bs 2,585 million for the second half of fiscal year 1959-60. The potential cash deficit of Bs 352 million is to be financed by drawing against the foreign commercial bank loan mentioned in paragraph 1 of this letter. Any increase in government cash balances above the level outstanding at the end of February, 1960, i.e. Bs 102 million, will be kept in the Central Bank.

conditions.text: Credit and monetary policy will be a strong complement to fiscal policy in bringing about the required adjustment in total domestic demand. In order to enable the Bank of Zambia to control better total domestic credit expansion and to slow down the increase in the monetary base, measures have been taken to reduce commercial banks' excess reserves by increasing their share in total bank lending to the mining companies and by absorbing whatever excess reserves are left by a sufficient increase in the reserve requirement. At the same time, interest rates on time and savings deposits have been increased by at least 1 percentage point, and commercial banks have been allowed to raise their interest rates on loans. Moreover, credit developments are being monitored much more closely than in the past, in particular by requesting commercial banks to provide promptly information on their loans categorised by major - 28 - ATTACHmENT B borrowers. In any event, total domestic credit (net),l/ which amounted to K 1,261 million at the end of 1977, will not exceed K 1,375 million during the period ending June 30, 1978, K 1,435 million during the period ending September 30, 1978 and K 1,490 million during the period ending December 31, 1978. conditions.text: Second, an orderly reduction and eventual elimination of external payments arrears in order to re-establish confidence abroad and reopen normal credit lines. Such arrears which are now estimated to reach SDR 467 million at the end of March 1978, will not exceed SDR 487 million at the end of June, 1978, SDR 442 million at the end of September, 1978, and SiR 397 million at the end of December, 1978. These ceilings will be lowered by the amount of any rescheduling of payments arrears for imports due to official creditors. Moreover, the Government intends to use a significant proportion of any export receipts in excess of the forecast level as well as of any balance of payments assistance over and above that requested from the Fund, to reduce such arrears. To ensure their orderly reduction, the Bank of Zambia has established a 100 per cent reserve requirement against such arrears, will closely monitor their repayment and, when their level has been reduced to more manageable proportions, will fully centralise them.

conditions.clause: the limits on the contracting or guaranteeing of any external borrowing by the Government, other than for the purpose of refinancing external payments arrears, with maturities of more than one year and less than five years or less than 15 years, as referred to in paragraph 14 of the memorandum annexed to the attached letter are exceeded; or
conditions.text: In view of the tight foreign exchange situation, Zambia intends to seek financial assistance from friendly governments, international organisations, and private banks. Moreover, the Government has established a special Commnittee in charge of carrying out a complete inventory of the existing external debt, of monitoring all loan transactions and commitments, and of developing appropriate external debt management policies. Because of the heavy external borrowing that we made in recent years, the Government will follow a cautious foreign Iorrowing policy in 1977-80. The contracting or guaranteeing of new external borrowing by the Government with an original maturity of more than one and up to fifteen years will be limited to SDR 280 million in 1978. Of this no more than SDR 50 million will be contracted or guaranteed with an original maturity of more than one and up to five years. However, loans contracted to refinance external payments arrears are excluded from these ceilings.

conditions.clause: the intention stated in the last two sentences of paragraph 15 of the memorandum annexed to the attached letter are not carried out
conditions.text: Although in 1978 Zambia is not yet in a position to relax existing restrictions on imports and current payments and transfers introduced for balance of payments purposes, measures are being taken to streamline the import system with a view to facilitating the importation of raw materials and essential consumer goods so as to permit enterprises to operate more efficiently and improve supply conditions. As the balance of payments improves, further relaxation measures will be taken in 1979, with the aim of eliminating restrictions introduced for balance of payments reasons by 1980. During the period of the proposed stand-by arrangement it is the Government's intention not to introduce any multiple currency practices or impose new or intensify existing restrictions on payments and transfers for current international transactions. Furthermore, the Government does not intend to introduce new or intensify existing restrictions on imports for balance of payments purposes.

conditions.text: We realize that in order to achieve the goals noted above, it is essential that liquidity in the economy be kept under constant surveillance. Since July 1964 by a series of measures we have successively tightened our credit policy. These measures, of which the latest were taken in March 1965, included raising our reserve requirements to the legal maximum, fixing limits for central bank credit to individual banks as well as tightening the conditions for granting credits to the economic organizations and the public authorities. Should the situation require, we will take further restraining measures. It is our intention to pursue our monetary policy in such a manner as to keep the rate of increase in money supply somewhat below the rate of increase in total economic activity. Such increase will be implemented in a selective manner in order to achieve our desired investment pattern, as well as to restrain the effect of the credit expansion on prices and on the balance of Payments.
